items.t: What algorithmic complexity means
items.s: Two solutions to the same problem both give the right answer. On 8000 items, one runs in 0.2 ms and the other takes 916 ms — **4000× apart**.

items.t: Big-O notation
items.s: Last lesson we said the nested loop "grows like n²". This lesson gives that claim a standard name and strict rules.

items.t: Comparing the common complexities
items.s: Line the usual complexities up and see how many orders of magnitude separate them.

items.t: Space complexity
items.s: Last lesson compared time. This one compares memory — **trading space for time** is the most common optimisation, but it isn't free.

items.t: Measuring complexity yourself
items.s: You analysed it as O(n²) — how do you check? **Run it and see what happens to the time when n doubles.** This lesson gives you a reusable way to measure.

items.t: Two Pointers: Why Brute Force O(n²) Collapses to O(n)
items.s: Two nested loops scan every pair. That is O(n²) — and for most array problems, most of those pairs are wasted work.

items.t: Collision Pointers: Reversing Arrays and Testing Palindromes
items.s: Once two pointers can search, they can also **swap**. That is all reversing really is.

items.t: Two Pointers, Different Speed: Removing and Deduplicating In-Place
items.s: Collision pointers are "two ends closing in." This lesson covers another shape: **the slow/fast pointer** — both move in the same direction, one scouts ahead while the other "records the answer."

items.t: The Sliding Window, First Steps: Smallest Subarray with a Given Sum
items.s: Slow/fast pointers are "one fast, one slow." This lesson upgrades that idea into a **sliding window**: the two pointers enclose an "interval," which you **expand** and **shrink** based on a condition.

items.t: Hands On: Taking Apart the Three-Sum Thought Process
items.s: Three-sum is an interview favorite and the most classic two-pointer exercise in practice. This lesson tears the thinking apart layer by layer: **sort first, then pin one and hunt for two**.

items.t: Why Preprocessing Matters: Range Sums from O(n) to O(1)
items.s: In the previous chapters we learned how two pointers can reduce dimensionality. This chapter takes a different angle: **preprocessing** — compute the answer in advance and store it, then fetch it directly when queried.

items.t: One-Dimensional Prefix Sums: Construction, Query, and the Leading Zero
items.s: Last lesson we learned that prefix sums can accelerate range queries. This lesson fills in every detail: **how to construct, how to query, and how to handle boundaries.**

items.t: 2D Prefix Sums: Submatrix Sums and the Inclusion-Exclusion Principle
items.s: 1D prefix sums handle interval sums. This lesson scales it up to two dimensions: **submatrix sums** — using inclusion-exclusion to answer in one shot.

items.t: Difference Arrays: Range Addition from O(n) to O(1), Plus Restoration
items.s: Prefix sums answer "what is the sum of a range?" This lesson covers its inverse operation: **difference arrays** — bringing "range addition" down from O(n) to O(1).

items.t: Real-World Practice: People-Flow Statistics (Multiple Range Overlays, One Restoration)
items.s: This lesson applies the difference array to a real scenario: **tracking how many people are present in each time slot** — overlaying many intervals, then restoring once at the end.

items.t: Why Binary Search Works: Monotonicity, and "Why It Has Ten Thousand Bugs"
items.s: In Chapter 1 we saw how fast binary search is (O(log n)). This chapter explains from scratch: **why binary search works, and why it is so easy to get wrong**.

items.t: Standard Binary Search: Closed-Interval Style, Computing Mid, and Infinite Loops
items.s: In the previous lesson we understood the prerequisites for binary search. This lesson gives a **reliable closed-interval template** and explains why each step is written the way it is.

items.t: Boundary Binary Search: Finding the First and Last Match
items.s: Standard binary search only answers "is it there?". This lesson solves the more common problem: **where is the first or last element that satisfies a condition in an ordered array?**

items.t: Binary Search on the Answer: Turning "Find the Optimum" into "Test a Candidate"
items.s: The first two lessons searched over **positions**. This lesson levels up: **binary search on the answer** -- if the answer itself is monotonic, we can binary-search it too.

items.t: In Practice: Searching in Rotated / Nearly Sorted Arrays
items.s: Standard binary search requires a fully sorted array. This lesson covers a classic variation: **rotated sorted arrays** -- mostly sorted, but with one "break point."

items.t: String Immutability: Why Concatenation in a Loop Is O(n²)
items.s: The first four chapters were all about arrays. This chapter moves on to strings — they look simple, but **string immutability** can quietly drag your code down.

items.t: Counting and Hashing: Character Frequency and Anagrams
items.s: The single most common operation on strings is **counting** — tallying how many times each character appears. This lesson covers it thoroughly.

items.t: Two Pointers on Strings: Reverse, Reverse Words, and Compress
items.s: The two-pointer patterns you learned for arrays work just as well on strings. This lesson works through three classics: **reverse, reverse words, and compress.**

items.t: Three Ways to Check a Palindrome: Center Expansion, Two Pointers, and Reverse-and-Compare
items.s: Palindromes are a frequent interview topic. This lesson covers three ways to check one, and compares their trade-offs.

items.t: Longest Palindromic Substring: From Brute Force to Center Expansion
items.s: In the previous lesson we saw that center expansion is the right tool for one job: **finding the longest palindromic substring**. This lesson derives the algorithm step by step.

items.t: What Is a Window: When to Use Sliding Window
items.s: Brute force enumerates all subarrays in O(n²); a sliding window crushes it to O(n). This lesson clarifies **when to reach for a window, when not to**, and how it relates to two pointers.

items.t: Fixed Windows: Maximum Sum of Size k and Moving Averages
items.s: Fixed windows are the gateway to all window techniques. The window length k stays constant; each slide is just "drop the leftmost, add the rightmost." This lesson breaks down the pattern and exposes a hidden performance trap.

items.t: Variable Windows: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
items.s: Fixed windows never change length; variable windows shrink on demand. This lesson uses "longest substring without repeating characters" as the battlefield to fully explain the **HashMap + left-boundary advance** technique.

items.t: Window + Counter: Minimum Window Substring
items.s: Fixed windows maintain a "sum"; variable windows maintain a "set." This lesson maintains a **counter**. We use `Counter` to track character frequencies inside the window with surgical precision and solve the "minimum window substring" class of exact-match problems.

items.t: Putting It All Together: Two Pointers, Prefix Sums, and Sliding Windows
items.s: Earlier lessons covered two pointers, prefix sums, and sliding windows in isolation. This lesson brings them into one toolbox: one **multi-technique** problem, plus a decision framework for choosing the right tool.

items.t: Why Linked Lists Exist: The Weakness of Arrays and the Strength of Linked Lists
items.s: In the previous chapters we squeezed every trick out of arrays: two pointers, prefix sums, binary search, sliding windows. But arrays have one built-in weakness—**insertion and deletion cost O(n)**. This chapter introduces the cure: linked lists.

items.t: ListNode and Hand-Built Linked Lists: Defining Nodes, Linking Them, Traversing and Printing
items.s: In this lesson we build a linked list from scratch: define a node, link nodes into a chain, then traverse and print it. Linked lists stop being abstract.

items.t: Insertion and Deletion: Head Insert, Middle Insert, Deleting a Node (Why You Need a Predecessor)
items.s: Insertion and deletion are where linked lists truly shine. This lesson breaks down head insertion, middle insertion, and deletion one by one, and explains why deletion absolutely requires the **predecessor**.

items.t: The Dummy Head Node: How It Eliminates the "Delete the Head" Special Case
items.s: The dummy node is the first linked-list technique, and the most important one: it makes the annoying special case of "deleting the head" disappear entirely.

items.t: Reversing a Linked List: The Iterative Version (Three Pointers), Frame by Frame
items.s: Reversing a linked list is the #1 interview question. This lesson hand-runs the `prev` / `cur` / `nxt` three-pointer approach frame by frame, laying out every arrow change in plain sight.

items.t: Fast & Slow Pointers: Find the Middle, Lay the Groundwork for Cycle Detection
items.s: The two-runner trick is a linked-list specialty. Two pointers leave the same starting line at different speeds, and that single idea unlocks finding the middle, detecting a cycle, and locating the k-th node from the end.

items.t: Cycle Detection: Why Floyd's Algorithm Always Meets
items.s: A linked list gives you no "end of the road" marker when a cycle exists—it just goes on forever. Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm answers "is there a loop?" in O(1) memory instead of O(n).

items.t: Merging Two Sorted Lists
items.s: Two already-sorted lists, one sorted result. This is the most-asked linked-list problem for a reason: it tests whether you can actually manipulate pointers without losing your place.

items.t: Removing the N-th Node From the End
items.s: Unlike an array, a linked list has no backward index. To delete the N-th node from the end in one pass, make two pointers keep a constant gap of N between them.

items.t: Case Study: The Design of an LRU Cache
items.s: An LRU cache is an interview litmus test: it demands O(1) lookup, O(1) move-to-front, and O(1) eviction from the tail. Neither a hash map nor a singly linked list can do all three—you need both.

items.t: What a Stack Is: Last In, First Out, and Why Python's List Already Is One
items.s: The stack is the simplest data structure in this book, and the most underrated. Parenthesis matching, undo, function calls, and expression evaluation all depend on it.

items.t: Matching Parentheses: The Textbook Use of a Stack
items.s: Given a string of brackets, decide whether they close correctly. This is the interview "entry ticket" for stacks, and a textbook demonstration of the "nearest match" idea.

items.t: Monotonic Stack: Next Greater Element
items.s: The question is: for every element, "who is the first element to my right that is bigger than me?" Brute force is O(n²); a monotonic stack does it in one pass at O(n). It is the most elegant use of a stack — the elements inside stay monotonic.

items.t: Recursion and the Stack: Call Stack, Stack Frames, and RecursionError
items.s: Recursion is not magic. Behind it is just a stack — every time you call a function, the system pushes a frame onto the "call stack"; when the function returns, that frame is popped. Once you understand this, `RecursionError` will never surprise you again.

items.t: Applied: Expression Evaluation and a Calculator
items.s: Given the infix expression `"3 + 5 * (2 - 4)"`, how do you compute the result? This is a comprehensive use of stacks — two stacks (an operand stack plus an operator stack), where operator precedence decides "who goes first".

items.t: Queues and Deques: The Art of FIFO
items.s: A queue is "waiting in line" — first come, first served. But using a Python list as a queue will bite you with O(n) in the most unexpected place. `collections.deque` is the real answer.

items.t: Circular Queues: Implementing a Queue with a Fixed Array
items.s: An interviewer favorite: given a fixed-size array, how do you implement a queue? The answer is a circular queue — two pointers that "wrap around" the array.

items.t: BFS and Queues: The Skeleton of Level-Order Traversal
items.s: BFS (Breadth-First Search) is the classic application of a queue. Its core idea fits in one sentence: "expand level by level." And "level by level" is exactly the FIFO semantics of a queue.

items.t: Monotonic Queues: Sliding Window Maximum
items.s: Given an array and a window size k, slide the window from left to right and ask "what's the maximum in the window" each time. Brute force is O(nk); a monotonic queue is O(n) — each element enters and leaves the queue exactly once.

items.t: Practice: Unweighted Shortest Path with BFS
items.s: BFS's most powerful application is finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Why does BFS find the shortest path? Because "arriving first" means "fewest steps." This lesson breaks it down completely.

items.t: What Is Hashing: From "Array Index" to "Key," the Cost of O(1)
items.s: A hash table is humanity's obsession with O(1). It turns everything into an array index and pretends it has infinite memory — the price is collisions and unpredictability.

items.t: Collisions and Resolution: Separate Chaining, Open Addressing, Load Factor, and Resizing
items.s: Collisions are the destiny of hash tables — squeezing an infinite world into a finite array guarantees a crash. But how you handle the crash decides whether your hash table is fast or slow.

items.t: Python's dict and set: Both Backed by Hash Tables
items.s: Python's `dict` and `set` are hash tables' "favorite children." Why did dict suddenly become ordered in 3.7+? Why can't a list be a key? The answers all live inside the hash table.

items.t: Hash Table Patterns: Two Sum, Counting, Prefix Sum + Hash
items.s: A hash table is one of the skeleton keys of algorithm problems. When you see "lookup," "dedup," "count," or "sum equals K," you should think hash table.

items.t: Practice: Grouping Anagrams
items.s: Grouping anagrams is a classic combination of hash tables and string processing. The core idea: find a way to **map anagrams to the same key.**

items.t: Recursion's Three Elements: Base Case, Recursive Relation, and Return Value
items.s: Recursion is not just "a function that calls itself." To write a correct recursive function you only need to answer three questions clearly: when to stop, how to break the big problem into a smaller one, and what to bring back once the smaller one is solved.

items.t: How Recursion Runs: the Call Stack, the Recursion Tree, and Print Debugging
items.s: The hardest part of recursion is not "writing it" but "seeing what it is doing." This lesson gives you three tools: the call stack, the recursion tree, and indented print. By the end of this lesson recursion will be transparent to you.

items.t: Turning Recursion into Iteration: When You Must Convert, and How
items.s: Recursion looks elegant when you write it and can blow up when you run it. This lesson covers three things: when recursion blows up, whether `sys.setrecursionlimit` really saves you, and three patterns for rewriting recursion as iteration.

items.t: Divide and Conquer: Writing Merge Sort Recursively
items.s: Divide and Conquer (D&C) is recursion's most natural application. It has only three steps: divide, conquer, combine. Merge sort performs these three steps to perfection, and it is also the best textbook for understanding where O(n log n) comes from.

items.t: Backtracking: Permutations and Combinations
items.s: Backtracking is recursion's most powerful application. Its template is just one sentence: **make a choice — recurse — undo the choice.** Get this one step right and permutations, combinations, subsets, Sudoku, and the eight queens all follow the same pattern.

items.t: What Is a Tree: Why Trees Exist at All
items.s: Arrays need O(n) to find an element; a sorted array gets lookup down to O(log n) but insertion costs O(n). A linked list inserts in O(1) yet still searches in O(n). A tree is the compromise in between: it bakes the "order" into the shape itself, so lookup, insertion, and deletion all run close to O(log n).

items.t: Binary Trees and Traversal: Preorder / Inorder / Postorder
items.s: Traversal means visiting every node in a tree exactly once. A binary tree only has three positions — left, root, right — and changing the order in which you visit them gives you the three classic traversals: preorder, inorder, and postorder. They are not just exam questions; they are the skeleton for every tree problem that follows.

items.t: Level-Order Traversal BFS: Why a Queue Layers Things Naturally
items.s: The first three traversals are all "plunge all the way down first" — depth-first. Level-order traversal is different: it visits one layer at a time, first all the nodes of layer 1, then layer 2... It relies on a queue. This lesson explains why a queue is naturally suited to分层.

items.t: Binary Search Trees (BST): Smaller on the Left, Larger on the Right — Search in O(h)
items.s: A BST is how "order" truly enters a tree structure. It stipulates that every node in the left subtree is smaller than the root, and every node in the right subtree is larger. This simple rule lets search, insertion, and deletion all walk one path to the bottom — and as long as the tree is not too skewed, that is O(log n).

items.t: Practice: Depth, Node Count, and Balance of a Tree
items.s: The first three lessons covered traversal; this lesson ties them together with three "quantities": maximum depth, total node count, and whether the tree is balanced. All three are "result from the subtrees + processing at the root," differing only in how they are combined.

items.t: The Universal Recipe for Tree Recursion: Split the Problem into "Left Subtree + Root + Right Subtree"
items.s: Tree problems look like they come in endless varieties, but their solutions all look the same: first ask "what do my left and right subtrees each give me," then ask "how do I combine their answers." This lesson turns that thinking into a template.

items.t: Path Problems: Root-to-Leaf Path Sums
items.s: "Paths" are the second major category of tree problems. This lesson covers the two most basic kinds: root-to-leaf path sums, and "does a path with sum equal to target exist." The core idea is to pass the "current path state" downward as a parameter.

items.t: Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)
items.s: The Lowest Common Ancestor is the classic "return a node" problem in tree questions: given two nodes p and q, find their deepest common ancestor. Its solution is remarkably elegant — a few lines of recursion hiding a clever divide-and-conquer idea.

items.t: Reconstructing a Binary Tree: From Preorder + Inorder
items.s: Given a tree's traversal results, can you restore the original tree? Preorder + inorder works, inorder + postorder works, but preorder + postorder does not. This lesson explains why, and walks through implementing a "preorder + inorder" reconstruction by hand.

items.t: Heaps and Priority Queues: Array Representation of a Complete Binary Tree, and heapq
items.s: A heap is a special kind of complete binary tree: a parent's value is always "no greater than / no smaller than" its children's values. Its killer application is the priority queue — you can grab the maximum or minimum element in O(1) at any time. This lesson covers its array representation and Python's `heapq`.

items.t: Graphs: Adjacency Matrix vs Adjacency List
items.s: Arrays are one-to-one, trees are one-to-many, and graphs are many-to-many. This lesson covers the basic elements of graphs and the two most common storage methods — adjacency matrices and adjacency lists — and when to use each.

items.t: DFS and BFS: Two Traversal Frameworks and Their Differences
items.s: There are only two ways to traverse a graph: Depth-First Search (DFS) and Breadth-First Search (BFS). DFS uses recursion (a stack) to plunge down one path; BFS uses a queue to expand level by level. This lesson drills both frameworks and explains when each is appropriate.

items.t: Topological Sort: Dependencies and Kahn's Algorithm
items.s: Topological sort solves the problem of "how to order tasks with dependencies". You must put on socks before shoes; you must finish a prerequisite course before taking the advanced one. Arranging these "before → after" relationships into a sequence is topological sorting. It only exists for Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs).

items.t: Disjoint Set Union: Connectivity and Path Compression
items.s: Disjoint Set Union (DSU) is the go-to tool for "dynamic connectivity": checking whether two nodes are connected and merging two sets. Its two optimizations — union by rank and path compression — bring each operation to nearly O(1).

items.t: Shortest Path: The Intuition Behind Dijkstra
items.s: How do you find the shortest path between two nodes in a weighted graph? BFS only works for unweighted graphs. Dijkstra is the answer — it uses a greedy strategy of "always pick the node with the current minimum distance" to progressively determine the shortest distance to every node. This lesson explains the intuition, not the proof.

items.t: The Lower Bound: Why Comparison Sorts Are Ω(n log n)
items.s: It is not that algorithms are not clever enough — the act of "comparing" itself carries only so much information. This lesson nails down that lower bound using a decision tree.

items.t: The Three Basic Sorts: Bubble, Selection, and Insertion
items.s: They are all O(n²) and look clumsy, but insertion sort can outperform many "fancy" algorithms when the data is nearly sorted. This lesson thoroughly dissects the essential differences among the three O(n²) sorts.

items.t: Merge Sort: Divide and Conquer, with Stability
items.s: Merge sort is the first truly O(n log n) sort, and it is **stable**. The cost is O(n) of extra space. This lesson goes from the divide-and-conquer idea to the merge operation, breaking it all down.

items.t: Quick Sort: The Partitioning Idea
items.s: Quick sort is the fastest general-purpose sorting algorithm in practice. C++'s `std::sort` and Java's primitive sort are both based on it. The core operation is "partitioning": pick a pivot and rearrange the array into "all smaller on the left, all larger on the right". This lesson thoroughly covers the Lomuto and Hoare partitioning schemes and explains why quick sort can degenerate to O(n²).

items.t: Heap Sort and Non-Comparison Sorting: Breaking the O(n log n) Barrier
items.s: The theoretical lower bound for comparison sorts is Ω(n log n) — you cannot do better than that. But counting sort, bucket sort, and radix sort do not need to compare element values. They exploit numerical range information in the data to achieve O(n). This lesson clarifies the distinction between heap sort and "non-comparison sorting".

items.t: What Is Dynamic Programming: Overlapping Subproblems & Optimal Substructure
items.s: Dynamic Programming (DP) is one of the most practical and high-frequency techniques in competitive programming. It breaks a "big problem" into "smaller problems," remembers the answers to those smaller problems, and reuses them—avoiding redundant computation and compressing exponential complexity into polynomial time.

items.t: State & Transition: How to Define the DP Array
items.s: "What does dp[i] mean?"—this is the hardest step in dynamic programming. Many students can write the code but have no idea what the dp array actually represents. This lesson walks you through defining the state and deriving the transition equation step by step.

items.t: 1D Dynamic Programming: House Robber & Longest Increasing Subsequence
items.s: 1D DP is the most common and fundamental form of dynamic programming. This lesson uses two classic problems—House Robber and Longest Increasing Subsequence—to help you fully grasp the 1D DP mindset.

items.t: 2D Dynamic Programming: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)
items.s: 1D DP only needs one index to describe a state; 2D DP needs two. This lesson uses Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) as a case study to clarify the meaning of the dp array, the filling order, and boundary handling in 2D DP.

items.t: Knapsack Problems: 0/1 Knapsack & Unbounded Knapsack
items.s: The knapsack problem is a classic application of dynamic programming. This lesson covers the two most fundamental variants: 0/1 Knapsack (each item can be used at most once) and Unbounded Knapsack (each item can be used infinitely). The core insight is understanding "why 0/1 knapsack requires reverse-order traversal."

items.t: How to Choose an Algorithm: Reverse-Engineering from Data Ranges
items.s: When you get a problem, don't rush to code. First check the data range, work backward to the maximum allowable time complexity, and then choose your algorithm. This is the most practical "problem-reading technique" for contests and interviews.

items.t: Greedy vs. DP: When Is Greedy Correct?
items.s: Greedy algorithms are much simpler to write than DP, but "greedy choice" isn't always correct. This lesson uses Activity Selection and Coin Change—two classic problems—to clarify why greedy works for some problems and fails for others.

items.t: Binary Search on Answer + Feasibility Check
items.s: Some problems ask for "what's the optimal value," which is hard to compute directly. But if you're given a candidate value X and asked "can the answer be ≤ X," it's often easy to check. Binary search on the answer is the classic technique that turns "find the optimum" into "check feasibility."

items.t: Prefix Sums + Hash + Sliding Window: Combined Techniques
items.s: Prefix sums, hash tables, and sliding windows are three fundamental tools. Each is simple on its own. But the truly difficult problems require combining them. This lesson uses classic problems to demonstrate how these three tools work together.

items.t: Capstone: One Problem from Brute Force → Optimization → Optimal
items.s: This lesson uses "Maximum Subarray Sum" to demonstrate the complete evolution from the most naive brute force through divide-and-conquer to the optimal solution. Learning this "step-by-step optimization" mindset will help you tackle new problems independently.
