items.t: Why lists aren't enough
items.s: You already know Python lists. So why learn NumPy?

items.t: Six ways to create an array
items.s: Typing `np.array([1,2,3])` by hand is only the start. In practice you far more often need to conjure a pile of numbers out of nothing.

items.t: dtype and shape
items.s: An array's values are only the surface. What really decides what it can do and how fast it runs are two properties: **type** and **shape**.

items.t: Basic array arithmetic
items.s: Arrays redefine what `+ - * /` mean. Get these new rules straight and everything after flows.

items.t: Lists vs arrays
items.s: Both hold a pile of numbers. How do you choose? This lesson gives a workable rule — and runs a real speed test.

items.t: Thinking in vectors
items.s: This lesson is the soul of NumPy: **learn to solve problems without loops**.

items.t: Universal functions (ufuncs)
items.s: NumPy has a large family of functions with exactly one job: **take an array, do the same thing to every element, return a new array**. They're called ufuncs.

items.t: Broadcasting
items.s: NumPy's most powerful — and most confusing — feature.

items.t: Broadcasting in practice
items.s: Rules understood — now see them at work. Two cases: **standardising data** and **distance matrices**.

items.t: Reading broadcast errors
items.s: Reading a `shape mismatch` is the dividing line between "can use NumPy" and "uses NumPy smoothly".

items.t: Slicing and views
items.s: NumPy's biggest landmine: **slicing does not copy data**.

items.t: Boolean and fancy indexing
items.s: Slices only take contiguous runs. To filter by condition or grab "items 1, 3 and 5", you need these two kinds of indexing.

items.t: Aggregation functions
items.s: Functions that turn many numbers into one statistic. This lesson tours the common ones and fixes one practical pain: **what to do when data is missing**.

items.t: What on earth is axis
items.s: NumPy's single most confusing idea. Grasp one sentence and it's clear forever: **axis is the dimension that gets collapsed**.

items.t: Practice: analysing grades
items.s: String all three chapters together and walk a complete analysis.

items.t: Joining arrays
items.s: Combining several arrays into one. Sounds simple, but "which direction" is surprisingly easy to get backwards.

items.t: Splitting arrays
items.s: The inverse of joining. Beyond "equal parts versus unequal", there's little to trip over here.

items.t: Repeating and tiling
items.s: `repeat` and `tile` both make arrays bigger, in completely different ways. A classic pair that trips people up.

items.t: Sorting and ranking
items.s: `sort` gives you sorted values; `argsort` gives you sorted **indices**. The latter is the one you'll actually use.

items.t: Unique values and set operations
items.s: Staples of data cleaning: drop duplicates, find what's shared, isolate what differs.

items.t: npy and npz
items.s: Saving computed data and loading it back. NumPy has its own binary format — far faster and safer than CSV.

items.t: Text files: savetxt / loadtxt
items.s: When the data needs to reach a person or a spreadsheet, you want CSV-like text.

items.t: Real CSVs: genfromtxt
items.s: `loadtxt` breaks on an empty field. Real data almost always has gaps, so `genfromtxt` is the one you'll reach for.

items.t: Common file-reading errors
items.s: When reading a file fails, the message usually names the cause. This lesson teaches you to read them.

items.t: End to end: from file to report
items.s: This lesson chains the previous four into a pipeline. It's what you actually do every day.

items.t: Project 1: monthly sales analysis
items.s: The first complete project. No new functions — just combining the first five chapters to solve a real problem.

items.t: Project 2: time series and moving averages
items.s: Share prices, temperature, daily active users — anything arranged in time needs a moving average sooner or later.

items.t: Project 3: an image is an array
items.s: A colour photo is, at bottom, a 3-D array. This lesson makes multi-dimensional arrays concrete.

items.t: Performance: avoid the slow idioms
items.s: No new API here — just one thing: **measured evidence of which idioms are slow, and by how much**.

items.t: From NumPy to pandas
items.s: The end of *Data Analysis 1* and the start of *Data Analysis 2*. This lesson states plainly **what NumPy can and cannot do**.

items.t: Why pandas
items.s: At the end of *Data Analysis 1* we said NumPy struggles with "text columns plus numeric columns". This lesson starts from that pain.

items.t: Series: a labelled column
items.s: Series is pandas' smallest unit. Understand it and a DataFrame is just "several Series together".

items.t: DataFrame: a table
items.s: Several Series together make a DataFrame. This lesson covers building one and the most common ways to do it.

items.t: Look at the data
items.s: You've been handed an unfamiliar table. What do you do in the first five minutes? This lesson gives you a fixed routine.

items.t: Reading CSV into a DataFrame
items.s: `read_csv` is the most-used function in pandas and the one with the most arguments. This lesson covers the useful ones and four classic traps.

items.t: Columns and rows
items.s: Chapter 1 said a DataFrame is "a dictionary of Series". This lesson covers getting things out of it — and one counter-intuitive rule.

items.t: loc versus iloc
items.s: The biggest source of confusion in pandas. Master this and half your future bugs never happen.

items.t: Filtering by condition
items.s: From "take everything" to "take only what matches". Boolean indexing, multiple conditions, and one syntax trap you will hit.

items.t: Changing values and adding columns
items.s: Once you can filter, you can start editing. Assignment, new columns, apply, and one famous warning.

items.t: Sorting and de-duplicating
items.s: The last two frequent operations: sort_values, drop_duplicates, and the "index travels along" caveat.

items.t: NaN and None
items.s: Real data always has gaps. This lesson explains what "empty" actually is in pandas — and one counter-intuitive property that silently breaks code if you don't know it.

items.t: Drop or fill
items.s: Once you've found the gaps, the first decision is: keep this row or not? This lesson covers dropna and fillna, and how to choose.

items.t: Type conversion
items.s: "It's clearly a number, so why can't I calculate with it?" — this lesson fixes the most frequent complaint in pandas.

items.t: Duplicates and outliers
items.s: Data isn't always missing — sometimes there's too much of it, or values are absurd. This lesson is about spotting both.

items.t: Working with text columns
items.s: You can't call Python string methods on a column directly — you need the `.str` accessor. This lesson covers cleaning dirty text.

items.t: Grouping: split-apply-combine
items.s: The first three chapters were about preparing data. This chapter is where you start asking questions — and the core move is `groupby`.

items.t: transform and filter
items.s: groupby usually returns something *shorter* than the original (one row per group). Sometimes you want the same length back — that's `transform`.

items.t: Multi-level indexes and reshaping
items.s: Grouping by several keys produces a "two-level index". This lesson is about living with it — a spot where many people get stuck.

items.t: Pivot tables
items.s: If you've used Excel's pivot tables, this is their pandas equivalent. If you haven't, it's essentially "group, then spread into a grid".

items.t: Putting it together: a sales report
items.s: Stringing the last four chapters into one real analysis pass. Not much new syntax here — the point is **order**.

items.t: concat: stacking tables top to bottom
items.s: `merge` joins side-by-side, `concat` stacks one on top of another. Get this distinction clear and you will never reach for the wrong tool again.

items.t: merge: joining tables four ways
items.s: Real data never lives in one table. Staff details sit in table A, salaries in B, departments in C — `merge` is the tool that brings them together by key.

items.t: Merge pitfalls: duplicate keys, naming clashes, and indicator
items.s: Merge most often goes wrong not with a syntax error, but with a result that "looks fine" while the numbers quietly double. This lesson is about catching those hidden mistakes.

items.t: melt: turning a wide table into a long one
items.s: Why reshape the same data at all? Because plotting and grouping both love long tables. `melt` is the tool that stands up values that are lying flat across columns.

items.t: pivot and pivot_table: standing a long table back up
items.s: `melt` flattens a wide table; `pivot` stands it back up. But pivot has a hard rule — duplicate combinations raise an error on the spot. When that happens, you need `pivot_table`.

items.t: Time series basics: from strings to a DatetimeIndex
items.s: Storing "2026-09-01" as a string lets you sort, but not "summarise by week." Once it becomes a real datetime, pandas' time magic actually kicks in.

items.t: resample: rebucketing data by time frequency
items.s: Daily data is too noisy; monthly trends are clearer. `resample` is the standard tool for regrouping "daily" data into "monthly," "weekly," or any other time bucket.

items.t: rolling: rolling windows and moving averages
items.s: Raw data jumps around too much to show a trend. A rolling window smooths out "the last N days" — and that is exactly what a moving average is.

items.t: shift and differencing: day-on-day, year-on-year, and growth rates
items.s: How much did we sell yesterday? The same day last year? Answering "how much changed, and by what percent" is not a recomputation — it is a matter of sliding the data along and subtracting.

items.t: Capstone: a complete data analysis report
items.s: You have now seen every tool in this course. This lesson strings them into one pipeline — from dirty data to a single conclusion, skipping no step along the way.

items.t: Why We Visualize: Anscombe's Quartet
items.s: Four tiny datasets with nearly identical statistics, yet four completely different stories on paper. This lesson answers a foundational question: if means and variances already summarize the data, why bother drawing a picture?

items.t: Figure and Axes: the Canvas and the Coordinate System
items.s: Writing `plt.plot(x, y)` is enough to get a picture, but as soon as you need multiple subplots, titles or different sizes, you must understand figure and axes. This lesson explains the two APIs in one pass.

items.t: Drawing Your First Line: `plot`, `marker`, `linestyle`, `color`
items.s: The line chart is the most commonly used visualisation in data analysis. This lesson unpacks the four core parameters of `plot` so that a single line can carry every style you want.

items.t: Fonts and Garbled Text
items.s: Chinese characters turning into boxes, minus signs turning into squares — every English user runs into this sooner or later when mixing scripts. This lesson explains the root cause and four solutions.

items.t: Saving and Exporting: the Pitfalls of `savefig`
items.s: Drawing is not the finish line — producing the file is. This lesson covers the four dimensions of `savefig`: size, dpi, bbox and format, so your output is sharp, uncropped and trouble-free.

items.t: Bar Charts `bar` / `barh`: Comparing Categories
items.s: The bar chart is the default choice for "which is bigger": which store sells more, which month performs best. This lesson covers the difference between `bar` and `barh`, and what to do when categories pile up.

items.t: Line Charts and Time Series: Trends and Dual Y-Axes
items.s: A line chart tells a "story of change": how sales move, how temperature shifts, how users grow. This lesson covers the correct way to draw time series and how to put "two different units" on one chart.

items.t: Scatter Plots: Two Variables and Mapping a Third Dimension
items.s: A scatter plot shows "how two variables move together". `scatter` is stronger than `plot` because it can colour and size each point independently — packing a third and fourth dimension into one chart.

items.t: Histograms and Box Plots: Seeing Distributions and Outliers
items.s: A mean only tells you "where the centre is"; a distribution plot tells you "what the data looks like". This lesson covers the histogram `hist` and the box plot `boxplot` — two powerful tools for looking at distributions.

items.t: The Pie-Chart Controversy and Its Alternatives
items.s: The pie chart is probably the first chart every beginner learns — and the one data-visualisation experts recommend least. This lesson explains why it is problematic and what to use instead.

items.t: Multi-panel layouts: subplots, shared axes, and tight packing
items.s: One figure with several panels is the standard shape of any analytical report. This lesson covers the three ways to build a `subplots` grid, how to share axes between panels, and when to call `tight_layout`.

items.t: Titles, axis labels, legends, and grids: make the plot self-explaning
items.s: If you hand a plot to someone with no background in your data, will they understand it? This lesson covers the four elements that make a figure self-explaining: title, axis labels, legend, and grid.

items.t: Annotations and reference lines: annotate, axhline, axvline
items.s: The one thing you most want your audience to remember is often a single point. This lesson shows how to mark that "key finding" with an arrow, a label, or a reference line.

items.t: Colour and style: colormaps, colour-blind safety, and seaborn themes
items.s: Colour choices determine how professional a plot looks. This lesson covers how to pick a colormap, how to avoid the colour-blind trap, and how one line of seaborn swaps the entire look of a figure.

items.t: Plotting directly from pandas: the df.plot() family
items.s: A DataFrame has its own `.plot()` method, so a usable figure is only a few lines away. This lesson covers where it is enough, where it falls short, and how to mix it with matplotlib.

items.t: Why seaborn: statistical plots with far less code
items.s: matplotlib can draw anything, but a good-looking plot with statistics behind it takes a dozen lines. seaborn sits on top of matplotlib and packs "aggregate, group, colour, confidence interval" into a single call.

items.t: Distribution plots: histplot, kdeplot, displot
items.s: The first thing you do with a dataset is not draw a relationship plot, it is **look at its shape**. A distribution plot answers "how often does this value occur, and where is the density concentrated".

items.t: Relational plots: relplot, scatterplot, lineplot, and grouping with hue
items.s: "Is there a relationship between these two variables?" is the question asked most often in data analysis. seaborn's relational plots combine "draw points or lines" with "colour by group" in one move, so a single line reveals group differences.

items.t: Categorical plots: boxplot, violinplot, barplot, countplot
items.s: When the horizontal axis is categorical and the vertical axis is numeric, you are not looking for "one number per category", you are looking for **the distribution inside each category**. That is exactly what the categorical plot family does.

items.t: Heatmaps and correlation matrices: heatmap, annot, and masking the upper triangle
items.s: Once variables pile up, drawing scatter plots one pair at a time is too slow. A correlation matrix tells you "who relates to whom" in one square, making it the fastest global scan in exploratory analysis.

items.t: From Question to Chart: Pick the Chart After You Know the Question
items.s: Most bad charts are not caused by bad code. They are caused by **drawing before you know what you are trying to answer**. This lesson gives you a decision table for "question → chart" and a full workflow from picking a topic to exporting the picture.

items.t: The Full EDA Flow: Shape, Missing Values, Outliers, Relationships
items.s: When you receive new data, do not model it and do not draw charts yet. Exploratory Data Analysis has four fixed steps. Walk through them in order and every later step becomes more reliable.

items.t: Charts That Lie: Truncated Axes, Dual Axes, Area Tricks and Hidden Sample Sizes
items.s: The same data can tell completely different stories depending on how you draw it. This lesson covers four of the most common visual deceptions and how to draw honestly instead.

items.t: Chart Readability: Information Density, Whitespace, Typography Hierarchy, One Idea Per Chart
items.s: A chart that runs is not the same as a chart that can be read. Readability is the engineering of "letting someone grasp the conclusion within 3 seconds", and it has four controls: information density, whitespace, type hierarchy and number of conclusions.

items.t: Putting It Together: One Deliverable Analysis Page
items.s: Take the previous 24 lessons and turn them into one complete artefact: an analysis page that fits on one A4 sheet, with three charts each stating one conclusion and a short paragraph of findings. This is something you can hand to someone else.

items.t: Receiving Dirty Data: Read, Overview, Set a Cleaning Strategy
items.s: Real data never arrives clean. This lesson is about the first 15 minutes after you receive a file: get it in, understand it, set a cleaning strategy. Get the order wrong and every later step is wasted effort.

items.t: Cleaning and Features: From Dirty Data to Usable Data
items.s: The previous lesson set the cleaning checklist; this one carries it out. Turn strings into numbers, fill or drop the missing values, hunt down the outliers, then derive a few new fields on the side. Cleaning is not tidying up - it is preparing food the model can actually eat.

items.t: Grouped Insights: Finding the Conclusions That Actually Matter
items.s: Once the data is read and cleaned, the real work begins: how to group it, how to aggregate it, how to rank it, and how to turn a pile of numbers into something you can say to your manager, like "London's average spend is 18% higher than New York's".

items.t: Visual Presentation: Turning Conclusions Into a Set of Charts
items.s: The previous lesson produced the conclusions; this one draws them. The core principle is just one line: **one idea per chart** - each chart answers exactly one question, and the charts must follow a logical order.

items.t: Writing the Report: Conclusions, Evidence, Limits and "What Data to Collect Next"
items.s: This is the final lesson of the book. By now you can read data, clean it, group it and draw charts - only one step remains: turn the work into a report that other people will actually read and dare to use. A good report = clear conclusions + verifiable evidence + honest limits + a pointer to what comes next.

items.t: Virtual Environments: Give Every Project Its Own Room
items.s: You have three projects on your machine: one needs Django 3, another needs Django 5, and a third is a script written three years ago whose dependencies nobody remembers. Without isolation they will eventually step on each other's toes — a virtual environment gives each project a separate room where they cannot interfere.

items.t: Dependency Management: From "Works on My Machine" to "Works Anywhere"
items.s: Alice sends you a project whose README says only "just pip install and run." You install, run it, and the first line raises `ImportError`. The code is not broken — nobody wrote down what it actually needs. Dependency management answers two questions: *what* do we need, and *which version*.

items.t: Beyond pip: uv and the Modern Toolchain
items.s: Running `pip install` makes you wait half a minute, then watch ten dependencies download one by one. Three people on the team end up with three different environments. The modern Python toolchain attacks exactly two pains — *slow* and *inconsistent* — and uv is the fastest runner in that race.

items.t: Project Layout: Helping a Newcomer Read Your Project in 30 Seconds
items.s: You open an open-source project whose root dumps `main.py`, `utils.py`, `test_main.py`, `data.csv`, and `config.ini` into the same folder. You want to change a feature and have no idea where to start. A good directory layout is a navigation map.

items.t: Configuration: Secrets, Feature Flags, and "Works on My Machine"
items.s: Alice hardcoded the database password in source and `git push`ed it — now the whole company can read it. Worse, production and staging share the same password. The core rule of configuration management is one line: **do not hardcode what changes.**

items.t: Naming and Readability: Names Are the UI of Your Code
items.s: You inherit a codebase and see `def p(data):` next to `def process_order_payload(payload):`. To understand the first you must read the entire body; the second you grasp at a glance. Code is read far more often than it is written — names are the manual you leave for your future self and your colleagues.

items.t: Function Design: One Job Per Function
items.s: You open a 400-line function that parses, validates, queries the database, sends email, and logs — all in passing. You want to change the retry logic when sending fails, but you are afraid to touch it because one change might ripple everywhere. Every problem in function design comes from one function doing too many things.

items.t: Comments and Docstrings: Say Why, Not What
items.s: You see a comment reading `# increment i`, followed by `i += 1`. It states the code's what — and anyone who can read Python already knows what `i += 1` does. A good comment tells **why**; a bad comment tells **what**.

items.t: Formatting and Linting: Let Tools Settle Style Arguments
items.s: Alice likes single quotes, Bob likes double quotes, Carol indents by two spaces, and you use four. Eighty percent of code review time goes to "should there be a space here?" Formatting tools exist to settle those arguments once and never discuss them again.

items.t: The Philosophy of Error Handling: Exceptions Should Not Be Seen — and Never Swallowed
items.s: Your API page starts告警 at midnight: 500 errors, and the logs hold only `Internal Server Error` — no stack trace, no context. It takes you four hours to trace it to an `except:` that swallowed the exception. The whole art of error handling lies in "catch when you can act, and let it bubble when you cannot."

items.t: The Basic Git Workflow: The add / commit / push Trio
items.s: You changed three files and want to commit. "git add . then git commit -m 'update' then git push" — that works, but it treats git like a file-syncing service. In a real workflow, every commit is a **meaningful node** that explains what you did and lets you roll back at any time.

items.t: Writing Good Commit Messages: "fix" Is Not Information
items.s: Six months from now you will search 5,000 commits for "the one that changed the login timeout." You run `git log --grep="fix"` and get 800 hits. A commit message is an index you build for your future self — `fix` is not an index.

items.t: Branching Strategy: Why You Must Not Edit main Directly
items.s: You edit main directly, push it, CI fails, and a colleague pulls half-written code that will not run. Worse, halfway through you realise the approach was wrong and want to undo — but main's history is already polluted. A branch exists for one reason: **keep work in progress separate from the version that works.**

items.t: .gitignore and the Things That Must Never Be Committed
items.s: `.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `.env`, `.DS_Store`, a 500 MB training-model file — once these enter the repository, a "few MB of source" instantly becomes "several GB of junk." `.gitignore` is the door that keeps them out.

items.t: Code Review: Not Fault-Finding, but Shared Responsibility
items.s: You open a PR and find twenty comments, fifteen of which say "missing a space here" or "bad variable name." You spend two days fixing formatting, and not one design issue gets discussed. Code review is the first gate of project quality; done wrong, it is a waste of time.

items.t: The Test Pyramid: Not Every Test Should Start From the UI
items.s: Your project has 200 tests, and every single one "launches a browser, clicks a button, and watches the page." A full run takes 40 minutes, CI is red every day, and nobody looks at it anymore. The more tests you add, the slower everything gets, until nobody even runs them locally — that is not a test suite, it is a burden. The test pyramid answers the question of "how many tests, and where do they live?"

items.t: pytest in Practice: Fixtures, Parametrization, and Test Isolation
items.s: You have 50 tests, each one copying the same "create the database, insert test data, tear down the database" block. Then the schema changes and you edit that block 50 times. Fixtures exist to remove exactly that repetition. And "tests leaking into each other" is the easiest trap to fall into.

items.t: Mocks and Monkey-Patching: Isolate External Dependencies, but Do Not Mock Everything
items.s: Your function makes an HTTP request, queries a database, and reads the system clock. Without mocks, your tests need the network, a running database, and a clock you cannot control — so they are slow and flaky. A mock is "a stand-in that replaces the real object." But over-mock and you stop testing real behavior and start testing the stand-in.

items.t: Coverage: 100% Does Not Mean Bug-Free
items.s: The report says "100% coverage" and you feel good. The next day production reports a bug: an empty-string username crashes everything. Coverage measures "was this code executed," not "was this code verified correct." Reading coverage means looking at **which line is not covered**, not staring at the percentage.

items.t: CI Basics: Why "It Worked on My Machine" Is Not a Strategy
items.s: You ran the tests locally, committed, pushed, merged. The next day a colleague pulls the code and the tests fail — their environment has a different `pandas` version. Later, someone forgets to run the tests and pushes; a bug lands on main. "It works on my machine" is the most useless sentence in software engineering, because it is not true on anyone else's machine. CI turns "build + check + test" into an action that runs on every commit.

items.t: Semantic Versioning: When to Bump major, minor, and patch
items.s: You made a small change and bumped the version from 1.2.3 straight to 2.0.0. Every project that depends on yours is now forced to check for a breaking change. A version number is not a counter that goes up whenever you feel like it; it is a **contract with your users**. Seeing 1.3.0 tells them it is safe to upgrade; seeing 2.0.0 tells them to expect code changes.

items.t: Packaging and Publishing: From Source to `pip install`
items.s: Your project is done and a colleague says "send it to me." You zip the whole directory, they unzip it, set up the paths by hand, and get an import error. That is what happens without packaging. Packaging turns a project into a standard, distributable form so anyone can install it with a single `pip install`.

items.t: Containers: Turning "It Runs on My Machine" Into "It Runs Anywhere"
items.s: A script that works on a colleague's laptop crashes on yours; CI passes but production explodes. Usually the code is fine and the environment is the problem. Docker packages the code together with its operating system, dependencies, and runtime, so "it runs on my machine" finally stops being a punchline.

items.t: Documentation: README, CHANGELOG, and Design Docs
items.s: Finishing the code is not the finish line. The moment someone else — including you, three months from now — can read it, run it, and change it without fear, that is delivery. Documentation is the part most often skipped and most often complained about. A good README gets a newcomer running in ten minutes; a bad README leaves a decent project untouched.

items.t: Capstone: Engineering an Existing Small Project
items.s: This is the chapter's capstone. The previous lessons covered versioning, packaging, containers, and documentation; this lesson ties them together. You take "a script that runs" and turn it into "a project that can be delivered." You will see the full改造 workflow — adding tests, CI, a README, a version, and a .gitignore — and how isolated topics combine into one finished deliverable.

items.t: Performance Basics: Measure First, Then Change
items.s: The first rule of optimization is "do not guess" — rewriting code on instinct usually changes nothing and sometimes introduces bugs. This lesson uses `cProfile` and `timeit` to find the real bottleneck before touching anything.

items.t: Logging and Observability: What Tells You Something Is Wrong in Production
items.s: `print` is fine for local development; it is not fine for production. Bugs in production disappear in an instant, and what you need is **searchable, traceable logs that can reconstruct one request end to end**. This lesson covers how to log, what to log, and **what must never be logged**.

items.t: Security Basics: Dependencies, Secrets, and Injection Defenses
items.s: Security is not a decoration added before launch; it is a habit baked in from the first line of code. This lesson covers three fundamentals that are easiest to overlook: how to scan dependencies for vulnerabilities, how to manage secrets, and how to defend against two fatal injection classes — SQL and command injection.

items.t: Deployment and Operations: From "Runs on My Machine" to "Runs in Production"
items.s: "It works on my machine" is the classic programmer joke and the most expensive kind of failure. This lesson covers the real gap between local and production: how to manage processes, how to know the service is alive, how to roll back when something breaks, and a **checklist that must be walked through before every release.**

items.t: Finale: The Full Ship-It Walkthrough, Then Your Own Project
items.s: Thirty lessons in, you now have every tool needed to turn "a script that runs" into "a project that can be delivered." This lesson strings them into a real release pipeline, gives you a **project health checklist you can actually check off**, and tells you where to go next.

items.t: From the Command Line to a Window
items.s: Every program you have written so far takes input from the keyboard and prints output to the terminal. A window program is different — it sets up a little "shop" and waits for the user to walk in and click things. This lesson explains exactly what problem a GUI solves.

items.t: Where tkinter Lives and How to Import It
items.s: In the previous lesson you saw `import tkinter as tk`. This lesson goes deep on that single line — why there are two flavors (`tkinter` and `tkinter.ttk`), what `Tk()` actually returns, and why `mainloop()` is not optional.

items.t: Window Properties
items.s: A bare gray window is ugly. This lesson is about dressing it up: title, size, whether it can be resized, minimum dimensions, icons, and the most useful trick of all — centering the window on the screen.

items.t: Your First Widgets: Label and Button
items.s: A window needs something inside it. This lesson covers the two most common widgets: Label (displaying text) and Button (clicking). The key point — and the part that trips everyone up — is that creating a widget does **not** mean it is visible; you must also "put it in."

items.t: Project: A Window That Says Hello
items.s: So far the material has been零散 (scattered) pieces of knowledge. This lesson ties them together: use Entry (input box) + Button (button) + Label (display) to build a small interactive program. The focus is on how the interface connects to the logic.

items.t: Overview of the Three Geometry Managers
items.s: A widget that has been created is "floating"; it needs to be placed inside a window before it has a position and a size. Three tools do that job: pack, grid, and place. This lesson explains the personality of each so you can pick the right one.

items.t: pack: Top, Bottom, Left, Right
items.s: pack is the simplest geometry manager, and the first one beginners get comfortable with. This lesson breaks down every pack argument so you know exactly where it works well — and where it falls short.

items.t: grid: Rows and Columns, rowspan/colspan, and sticky
items.s: grid is tkinter's most commonly used and most flexible geometry manager. This lesson covers it thoroughly: rows and columns, spanning rows and columns, sticking to edges, and margins. Master grid and you can build 80% of any interface.

items.t: grid Weight: Why Widgets Refuse to Move When the Window Grows
items.s: This is the single most frustrating problem in tkinter: you enlarge the window and the widgets stay stubbornly glued to their original positions. This lesson explains `rowconfigure` / `columnconfigure` and the `weight` property. Once you understand it, your interfaces will scale with the window.

items.t: place: Absolute and Relative Positioning
items.s: place is tkinter's most "primitive" layout method — it assigns coordinates directly. This lesson covers how to use it, why it is usually not recommended, and the rare situations where nothing else will do.

items.t: Entry: The Single-Line Input Box — `get`, `delete`, `insert`
items.s: Entry is the workhorse of every login screen, search bar, and settings dialog. It holds exactly one line of text. This lesson covers its four core methods — `get`, `delete`, `insert`, `index` — plus `StringVar` and `trace`, the pair that turns a plain input box into a living piece of your program's data.

items.t: Text: The Multiline Widget — `insert`, `get`, `delete`
items.s: Entry handles one line. The moment you need a chat log, a code editor, or a paragraph of notes, you need Text. This lesson covers Text's quirky index system (why `"1.0"`?), how to read and write it, and how to make a read-only "log window" with coloured output.

items.t: Checkbutton and Radiobutton
items.s: Pick one of several options, or any number of them — that's the job of Radiobutton and Checkbutton. This lesson explains why tkinter forces you to use variable classes (`BooleanVar`, `IntVar`, `StringVar`) and how the same variable is what makes "pick one" actually mean "pick exactly one".

items.t: Listbox and Scrollbar
items.s: Once your options outgrow a handful of Radiobuttons, you need a list. This lesson covers Listbox (add items, read the selection, multi-select) and Scrollbar — including the two-way binding that everyone gets wrong the first time.

items.t: Combobox, Spinbox, Scale: The ttk Widgets
items.s: The default tkinter widgets look like Windows 95, on purpose — they were designed in the nineties. ttk (themed Tk) gives you widgets that match the user's operating system, plus three widgets tkinter never had: Combobox, Spinbox, and Scale. This lesson covers all three, and why reaching for ttk is usually the right call.

items.t: The `command` Callback: What Happens When You Click
items.s: A button that does nothing is just a label with an attitude. This lesson is about the function behind the button: why `command=greet()` is a disaster, what `command=` actually accepts, and how a callback reaches back into the widgets on screen.

items.t: `lambda` and Passing Arguments
items.s: `command` only takes callables with zero arguments, but callbacks almost always need data. `lambda` is the bridge — a way to manufacture a zero-argument function on the spot. This lesson also covers `functools.partial`, the gotcha that catches every tkinter learner, and when you should stop using lambda entirely.

items.t: `bind` and Event Sequences
items.s: `command` covers clicks on a handful of widgets. Everything else — mouse movement, key presses, double-clicks, window resizing — goes through `bind`. This lesson covers event sequences, the difference between widget-level and global bindings, and the `event` object that arrives with every callback.

items.t: Keyboard and Mouse: Focus, Shortcuts, and Drag
items.s: This lesson fills in the parts of input handling that `bind` only hints at: who receives keyboard events, how to wire up shortcuts, and how to make something draggable. Along the way it covers the three-mouse-event recipe that nearly every drawing and game program in tkinter ends up using.

items.t: Variable Tracing With `trace`: Update as You Type
items.s: Buttons make things happen after a click. `trace` makes things happen the instant a variable changes — no button required. This lesson explains the three trace modes, the callback signature tkinter expects, and uses both to build a calculator that updates while you type.

items.t: Pop-Up Dialogs: `messagebox`
items.s: A GUI program needs to talk to the user sometimes — to confirm a risky action, report a problem, or ask a yes/no question. `tkinter.messagebox` gives you a handful of ready-made pop-up windows so you don't have to build them from scratch.

items.t: Opening and Saving Files: `filedialog`
items.s: A text editor that can't open a file isn't an editor. `tkinter.filedialog` gives you the same "open file" and "save as" windows you've seen in every desktop program — the user navigates folders, picks a file, and your code gets a path string back.

items.t: Asking for One Value: `simpledialog`
items.s: Sometimes you don't need a whole form — you just need the user to type a name, a number, or a password. `tkinter.simpledialog` is the quickest way to pop up a single-input box and get one value back.

items.t: Menus: Main, Dropdown, and Right-Click
items.s: Every real desktop program has a menu bar across the top: File, Edit, Help. `tkinter.Menu` builds those, plus dropdown submenus and the right-click context menu. Once you learn the three-step recipe, all three kinds fall out for free.

items.t: Extra Windows with `Toplevel` (and Modal vs Non-Modal)
items.s: One window is rarely enough. A settings panel, a help box, a confirmation sheet — these all want to be separate windows. `tkinter.Toplevel` makes a second (or third) window, and with `grab_set()` you can make it modal: the user has to deal with it before going back to the main window.

items.t: Planning a Real Program: The Text Statistics Tool
items.s: Lessons 1-25 taught you the pieces. Now you'll build something real: a tool that loads a text file and counts characters, words, lines, and how often each word appears. Before writing any code, this lesson is about turning a vague idea into a checklist you can actually implement.

items.t: Laying Out the Interface with `Frame` and `grid`
items.s: Lesson 26 gave you a sketch of the text-statistics tool. This lesson turns that sketch into real widgets, organised into `Frame` panels and placed with `grid`. The rule is simple: divide first, place second, and never mix `pack` and `grid` inside the same container.

items.t: Separating Logic From the Interface
items.s: The counting code belongs in plain functions; the widgets belong on screen. Lesson 28 is about keeping that boundary clean, so you can change the interface without breaking the maths, and test the maths without opening a window.

items.t: Wiring Up File Reading
items.s: The layout exists, the logic is separate, the bridge method is written. Lesson 29 connects the last piece: picking a file, reading it safely, and pushing the text through `count_stats` and `top_words` to the screen.

items.t: Finishing Touches and What to Learn Next
items.s: The program works on the happy path. Lesson 30 is about the cases that aren't happy: the file doesn't exist, the encoding is wrong, the user clicks Analyse on an empty editor, or the file is 80 MB and the interface freezes. Then we'll look at where tkinter stops and the rest of the Python GUI world begins.

items.t: What Is a Canvas: A Blank Area You Can Draw On
items.s: So far, every widget we have used was a ready-made component — a button is a button, a label is a label. But what if you want to draw a circle, sketch a line, or build a draggable slider? That is where the Canvas comes in. It is the most flexible widget tkinter offers.

items.t: Drawing Basic Shapes: Rectangles, Ovals, Lines and Polygons
items.s: In the previous lesson we met the canvas; in this one we start drawing for real. tkinter provides a small set of simple drawing commands, and learning these few is enough to produce most interface elements.

items.t: Drawing Text and Images: create_text and PhotoImage
items.s: A canvas can hold more than geometric shapes — it can also display text and images. This lesson covers the two most common "content" drawing methods, along with a classic tkinter trap.

items.t: Manipulating Shapes: move, coords, itemconfig and tag
items.s: A shape does not have to sit there once it has been drawn. This lesson covers four core operations — move it, change its coordinates, alter its properties, delete it — and how to manage a group of shapes using "tags".

items.t: Project: A Drawing Pad That Draws and Clears
items.s: The previous lessons covered Canvas drawing and manipulation in pieces. This one ties them together into something genuinely useful — a drawing pad you control with the mouse. The core pattern is "event plus coordinates plus a line".

items.t: The after() Timer: Why You Must Not Use while True for Animation
items.s: When you want something to move on screen, the first idea is often "just add a loop". But in a GUI program, `while True` will freeze the interface outright. This lesson introduces tkinter's proper timing mechanism: `after()`.

items.t: Making Shapes Move: after Plus move, and a Bouncing Ball
items.s: In the previous lesson we learned `after`; in this one we use it to build a complete animation — a ball that bounces around inside the canvas. The whole recipe is "nudge it a little each frame and bounce on contact".

items.t: Frame Rate and Delta Time: Why a Fixed Step Runs at Different Speeds
items.s: In the previous lesson we animated by "moving 4 pixels per frame". But that hides a problem: on different machines and under different loads, the frame rate varies, so the animation speed changes too. This lesson introduces "delta time", which makes an animation run at the same speed on any machine.

items.t: Keyboard Control: Binding Key Events to Move a Square with the Arrow Keys
items.s: Games need keyboard control. This lesson covers tkinter's keyboard-event bindings and builds a square that moves using the arrow keys.

items.t: Project: A Simple Pong Game
items.s: This lesson combines animation, keyboard input and collision detection into a playable pong game: the ball bounces, the paddle is moved with the arrow keys, you score a point for catching the ball and lose one when it gets past you.

items.t: What Is ttk: Why Native Widgets Look Dated and ttk Gives You Themed Widgets
items.s: Up to now we have used tkinter's "native widgets" (tk.Button, tk.Label), which look plain and differ between Windows, macOS and Linux. ttk is tkinter's themed widget library, producing interfaces that are smarter and more consistent.

items.t: ttk Themes and Styles: Style, theme_use and configure
items.s: In the previous lesson we learned that a ttk widget's appearance is managed by a theme. This lesson covers how to switch themes and how to customise widget styles with `ttk.Style()`.

items.t: The Treeview Table: Columns, Rows, Inserting Data and Selection Events
items.s: ttk's Treeview is a "tree-plus-table" widget. It can act as a tree (expandable and collapsible hierarchy) or as a table (multiple columns and rows). This lesson focuses on the most common use: building a table to display data.

items.t: Notebook Tab Pages: A Multi-Page Interface
items.s: When one window has too much content, piling it all together gets crowded. Notebook provides "tabbed" switching, placing different functions on different pages — the same idea as browser tabs.

items.t: Progressbar and Progress Feedback: Keeping the Interface Responsive During Long Work
items.s: When a program does background work (downloading, calculating), the user needs a "progress bar" to know how long is left. This lesson covers ttk.Progressbar and the correct way to keep a tkinter interface responsive during long-running work.

items.t: Why Games Use pygame: The Limits of tkinter for Game Development
items.s: You've learned a lot about tkinter — you can make drawing apps and bouncing balls. But when it comes to real games, everyone recommends pygame. This lesson explains "why", helping you understand where each library fits.

items.t: Installation and Your First Window: pygame.init, display.set_mode, and the Quit Event Loop
items.s: From this lesson we enter pygame. We'll install the library, create a window, and write a "minimum runnable program" that closes properly — the starting point for every pygame project.

items.t: The Game Loop's Three Jobs: Handle Events, Update State, Redraw
items.s: Last lesson we built the minimum window. This lesson breaks the game loop into "three jobs" and uses it to make a small box that moves across the screen — understand this structure and every game you build will follow the same pattern.

items.t: Drawing Shapes and Loading Images: Surface, blit, and the Coordinate System
items.s: Last lesson used pygame.draw for basic shapes. This lesson dives into the "Surface" concept, teaching you how to load images, paste them onto the screen (blit), and understand pygame's coordinate system.

items.t: Frame Rate Control: Clock and tick, and Why You Shouldn't Run at Full CPU
items.s: The game loops from earlier lessons "work", but is faster always better? This lesson covers `pygame.time.Clock` — locking your game's frame rate, saving CPU, and understanding the relationship between "frame rate" and "speed".

items.t: Sprite and Group: Why We Need Sprite Classes
items.s: Previously we managed a character with a bunch of variables (x, y, speed, color). As characters multiply and logic grows, this "scattered state" becomes unmanageable. This lesson introduces pygame's Sprite and Group, using object-oriented principles to manage game objects.

items.t: Movement and Boundaries: Velocity Vectors and Boundary Detection
items.s: Last lesson covered Sprites. This lesson makes "movement" more规范: managing motion with velocity vectors (vx, vy), encapsulating boundary detection into methods, and keeping sprite movement logic clean and reusable.

items.t: Collision Detection: rect.colliderect and spritecollide
items.s: The most common need in games: "Did the ball hit the paddle?" "Did the bullet hit the enemy?" This lesson covers pygame's collision detection tools — from the simplest Rect collision to批量 detection between sprite groups.

items.t: Handling Keyboard Input: Continuous Keys and key.get_pressed
items.s: tkinter keys are "press once, fire once" — useless for "hold direction key to keep moving". pygame provides two approaches: event-style (KEYDOWN/KEYUP) and state-style (key.get_pressed). This lesson covers how to use state-style input for smooth continuous movement.

items.t: Project: Catch Game (Paddle + Ball + Score)
items.s: Let's tie together Lessons 18–24 and build a complete catch game: a paddle moved with arrow keys, a ball falling randomly, catch it for points, miss it and lose a life, with start and end screens.

items.t: Sound and Text: Making Your Game Speak and Play
items.s: So far your game has been "mute" — just drawing boxes. This lesson adds sound effects and text: a "ding" when collecting coins, and "Game Over" displayed on screen.

items.t: State Management: Using One Variable to Switch Between Start, Playing, and Game Over
items.s: Your first game only had one state: "playing". But real games have start menus, pause screens, and result screens. This lesson covers how to use **one `state` variable** to connect all these screens.

items.t: Saving and Config: Storing the High Score in a File
items.s: When you close and reopen the game, your score is gone — that doesn't motivate a second playthrough. This lesson teaches you how to write data (high score, settings, progress) **to a file and read it back**, and how to do it without crashing on a corrupted file.

items.t: Common Crashes and Debugging: Fixing "Frozen" and "Black Screen"
items.s: The previous lessons covered "how to write it right". This lesson covers "how to fix it when you write it wrong" — windows freezing, images not found, keys unresponsive, and confusing Rect and Surface. These are the four biggest crash scenarios for pygame beginners.

items.t: Final Project: A Complete Mini-Game and What to Learn Next
items.s: The previous five chapters covered sprites, collision, sound, state, saving, and debugging. This lesson **brings it all together** into a complete mini-game that you can play, save scores in, with a menu, sound effects, and an end screen — and tells you where to go from here.

items.t: What We Are Building: A Requirements List for a Ledger
items.s: In the first two books you learned to "make parts" — buttons, entries, canvases, tables. In this book you will "assemble a machine": a real, working desktop application. The first thing to do is **not** to write code. It is to figure out exactly what you are building.

items.t: Designing the Data Model: What Fields Does a Record Have?
items.s: The previous lesson set out "what we are building". This lesson sets out "what the data looks like". The data model is the foundation of the whole project — once it is decided, the database table, the interface fields and the reporting dimensions all follow from it.

items.t: Slicing the Modules: A Three-Layer Architecture
items.s: Requirements? Done. Data model? Done. Now it is time to write code. The first decision is **not** to build the window, but to split the code into three layers: data, interface and logic. This lesson explains why to separate them, and how.

items.t: A Prototype Sketch: Draw the Interface Before You Code
items.s: The code is now layered. One last thing before you start: draw what the interface will look like. Not with design software — with ASCII characters on paper. First settle "what the user sees and where they click", then decide "how many widgets go in the code".

items.t: Technology Choices: Why SQLite?
items.s: This lesson locks in the entire technology stack for the book: where the data is stored, which library draws the charts, whether any third-party packages are needed. Once this lesson is done, the next five chapters are about filling in the details of these choices.

items.t: SQLite and Connections: The sqlite3 Standard Library
items.s: This lesson begins the data layer. SQLite is the data heart of this book — every record you write and every statistic you calculate passes through it. The first lesson is simply "how to connect to it".

items.t: Creating Tables: CREATE TABLE
items.s: Connections are covered. This lesson turns the data model from lesson 2 into real SQL `CREATE TABLE` statements. Whether the table is designed well decides whether every later query is smooth or awkward.

items.t: CRUD: INSERT / SELECT / UPDATE / DELETE
items.s: The table exists. This lesson covers all four core operations at once — Create, Read, Update and Delete, or CRUD. They are the whole foundation of the data layer; every later interface action is really a call to one of these four.

items.t: Parameterised Queries: Why SQL Must Not Be Concatenated
items.s: Every SQL statement in the previous lesson used `?` placeholders. This lesson explains why — because string concatenation in SQL is a fatal security hole, and even if "this program is just for you" it pays to build good habits.

items.t: Transactions and Connection Management
items.s: This lesson closes out the data layer: what exactly do commit and rollback manage, and when should the connection be opened and closed? Get these two right and your program will not suffer from "data mysteriously disappears" or "the file is locked".

items.t: The Main Window and a Three-Layer Layout
items.s: The data layer is done. From this lesson on, the interface is built. This lesson does exactly one thing: create the main window, slice it into top, middle and bottom with `pack`, and ignore what widgets go inside. Get the skeleton right and adding pieces later is easy.

items.t: The Treeview Table: Column Definitions and Filling Data
items.s: This lesson replaces the placeholder Frame in the middle with a real table — ttk.Treeview. It is the widget in tkinter that feels closest to a "professional application", and the ledger's record list depends on it entirely.

items.t: The Entry Form: Label + Entry + Combobox + Button
items.s: The table is working. This lesson builds the bottom entry area: four input controls for date, amount, category and note, plus an "Add entry" button. The form is where the user interacts with the software most often, so getting it right decides the whole experience.

items.t: Input Validation: The Amount Must Be a Number, the Category Cannot Be Empty
items.s: The form accepts input now, but users will type anything: "abc" in the amount box, "yesterday" in the date box, or a blank category before clicking save. This lesson blocks that "dirty data" before it reaches the database.

items.t: Empty States and Feedback: What to Show When There Is No Data
items.s: A detail often overlooked: the first time the program starts and the database is empty, the table is a blank space. An empty table cannot speak for itself, and the user is simply confused — this lesson covers how to handle the "empty state".

items.t: Wiring Up the Data Layer: Loading Records into a Treeview
items.s: The last three lessons gave you the interface skeleton. This lesson makes the first real connection: when the program starts, it reads the database automatically and fills the table. There is no entry feature yet, but you will see real data appear on screen.

items.t: Adding a Record: From Form to Database and Back to the Table
items.s: This lesson closes the first complete loop: the user fills in a form, clicks "Add", the data lands in the database, and a new row appears in the table. This is the single most important connection in the whole application.

items.t: Deleting and Editing: Select a Row, Confirm, Act, Refresh
items.s: Entry is done. This lesson adds the two remaining operations: delete and edit. They share one requirement: "select a row first". So the focus is the Treeview selection mechanism, and why the iid must be the database id.

items.t: Decoupling with the Observer Pattern: Notifying the Interface When Data Changes
items.s: The last three lessons made us call `refresh_table` by hand after every write. Miss one and you get a bug; write it three times and it is redundant. This lesson automates "refresh" with the observer pattern, so the display updates the moment the data changes and you never have to remember to call refresh again.

items.t: Refresh Strategies: Full Refresh Versus Incremental Update
items.s: Lesson 19 made the display refresh whenever data changes. This lesson answers a performance question: when you refresh, do you wipe the whole table and redraw it, or do you touch only the changed row? Both strategies have their place, and mixing them up gives you either a freeze or a wrong display.

items.t: Summarising by Category with SQL GROUP BY
items.s: Statistics start here. Requirement F3 is "see where the money went", and the first step is to aggregate the data into "how much was spent in each category". We have two routes: SQL's GROUP BY and pandas. This lesson covers the SQL route — it lives in the standard library, with zero dependencies.

items.t: Embedding matplotlib in tkinter with FigureCanvasTkAgg
items.s: The aggregation is done. This lesson turns the result into a chart. matplotlib is the one third-party library we must bring in, and it can embed natively inside a tkinter window — provided you use `FigureCanvasTkAgg` and **never** `plt.show()`.

items.t: Pie Charts and Bar Charts: Category Share and Monthly Trends
items.s: Last lesson embedded a chart in the window. This lesson draws the two most useful statistical graphics: a pie chart to show category share, and a bar chart to show a monthly trend. The data all comes from lesson 21's aggregation functions.

items.t: Chinese Fonts: Fixing the Square Boxes in Chart Text
items.s: You label a chart with a Chinese title and what you get is `□□□` — a row of boxes. This is not a bug, it is a font that has no Chinese glyph. This lesson fixes it once and for all, and explains how matplotlib font configuration actually works.

items.t: Keeping Charts in Sync: Auto-Refresh When the Data Changes
items.s: You edit a record, switch to the statistics tab, and the pie chart still shows the old data — because it was only drawn once. This lesson links aggregation, drawing, and refresh into one chain, so the chart recomputes and redraws after every add, edit, and delete. It is the last step that turns the statistics page from "viewable" to "usable".

items.t: Exception Handling and Fallbacks: Never Let the Program Crash on the User
items.s: The disk is full, a colleague deleted `ledger.db`, someone typed "abc" in the amount box — these things will happen. This lesson fits your ledger with a "safety belt": a global exception hook catches what escapes, a full disk gets a message, bad input gets validation, and the user never sees a wall of red errors.

items.t: Configuration and Preferences: Remembering Window Size and the Last-Opened File
items.s: You close the ledger and reopen it: the window is back to 800×600, the statistics tab selection is gone, and you have to find the ledger file all over again. That "memory" is configuration. This lesson covers where the config file belongs (a cross-platform path), what to store, how to read it, and why pickle is the wrong choice for preferences.

items.t: Packaging: Turning the Ledger Into a Double-Clickable Executable
items.s: The code is finished and your mum wants to use your ledger. You cannot exactly ask her to install Python, then tkinter, then matplotlib, then `git clone` your repo. This lesson packages the whole project into a single executable, and explains why it is not as simple as it sounds.

items.t: Slimming Down: Cutting a 60MB Executable to 30MB
items.s: A tkinter program that just says "Hello World" comes out around 10MB after PyInstaller. Add matplotlib for two charts and it jumps past 60MB. This lesson explains where the size actually goes, and how to use `--exclude-module` and careful investigation to bring it back down.

items.t: Release and Wrap-Up: Shipping the Ledger and Moving On to Qt
items.s: The code is done, the build works, and the bundle is down to 30MB. Now comes the act of delivery itself — an exe with no README, no version number, and no licence is indistinguishable from a folder of random files in the user's eyes. This lesson covers the release checklist, looks back at what you have actually completed, and points out where to go next.

items.t: What Programming Actually Is
items.s: No code in this lesson. Let's get the essence straight first — when you get stuck in the 25 lessons ahead, you'll find most of the confusion traces back to something not fully clicked here.

items.t: Making the Computer Understand You
items.s: Before writing code you need somewhere to run it. This lesson sorts that out properly, and walks you through installing the editor.

items.t: Your First Program
items.s: Finally, code. This lesson covers exactly one thing — `print`. But I'll break it down far enough that you know what every bracket and every quote is for.

items.t: Writing for Humans
items.s: Comments don't make programs run faster. They stop you from collapsing three months later. This lesson covers why they matter and how to write them without wasting them.

items.t: Errors Don't Mean You're Wrong
items.s: Beginners fear red error text; veterans love it. This lesson resets your relationship with errors — they're a free, 24/7, extremely patient tutor.

items.t: Variables: giving data a name
items.s: In chapter 1 every program was disposable — it printed something and ended, leaving nothing behind.

items.t: Numbers: integers and floats
items.s: Python has two common kinds of number. The difference between them is subtle, but getting it wrong causes real bugs.

items.t: Strings: working with text
items.s: Programs don't handle numbers only. Names, addresses, a sentence, a whole article — in Python all of these are **strings**.

items.t: Booleans and comparisons
items.s: One data type has only two values, yet it is the foundation of every decision a program makes.

items.t: Otherwise: `else`

items.s: `if` / `else` handles "one of two." But real life is usually **one of many.**

items.s: Last lesson's `while` had a prerequisite: **you need to know in advance when the condition becomes false.**

items.t: One Box, Many Values: Lists
items.s: So far every variable you have written holds exactly **one** thing — one score, one name, one number.

items.t: Indexes: Reaching in by Position
items.s: A list can hold a whole pile of values, but stuffing them in is useless if you cannot **take one back out**.

items.t: Adding and Removing: Making a List Grow and Shrink
items.s: An index can only change a position that **already exists**. But real programs collect data as they run — each time the user submits a form, there is one more item.

items.t: Slicing: Grabbing a Whole Segment at Once
items.s: An index can only fetch one element at a time. But often what you want is **a segment**: the first three scores, the last two names, or everything from the second to the second-to-last.

items.t: Iteration and Common Operations: Actually Using a List
items.s: The previous four lessons answered "how do I store, fetch, and change values". This one answers the final question: **how do I do something to the whole pile at once?**

items.t: Tuples: Lists That Cannot Change
items.s: A list can grow, shrink, and be rewritten at will. But some data is **never meant to change** — the coordinates of London, someone's name, the fact that a year has twelve months.

items.t: Tuple Unpacking: Assigning to Several Names at Once
items.s: Lesson 6 said "a tuple is defined by its commas". This lesson covers the single biggest convenience that commas bring: **taking the values inside a tuple and handing them to several variables at once.**

items.t: Strings Are Immutable
items.s: Lesson 3 taught you that you can replace an element by position: `nums[0] = 99`. You might wonder whether, since a string is just a sequence of characters, you can write `s[0] = 'X'`.

items.t: String Formatting: Slipping Data into Strings
items.s: In earlier lessons you have probably written code like this:

items.t: The Family Resemblance: list, tuple, and str Are Sequences
items.s: The last four lessons covered lists, tuples, and strings separately. You have probably noticed they feel **very alike** — all can be indexed, sliced, and measured for length.

items.t: Why Dictionaries Exist: Look Up by Name, Not by Position
items.s: Everything we have stored so far — lists and tuples — is fetched by **position**: `scores[0]` is the first item, `scores[1]` is the second.

items.t: Dictionaries: Create, Read, Update, Delete
items.s: The previous lesson covered creating a dictionary and reading values by key. This lesson treats the dictionary as a **mutable container** — adding an entry, changing one, removing one, looking one up — plus a few methods designed to save you trouble.

items.t: Iterating Dictionaries and Other Common Operations
items.s: So far we have handled one dictionary entry at a time. This lesson is about **batch** operations: how to walk through every key, value, and key-value pair, plus the error you are almost certain to hit.

items.t: Dictionary Pitfalls: Keys Must Be Hashable, and Do Not Rely on Order
items.s: Dictionaries are pleasant to use, but there are three traps almost everyone hits. This lesson walks through all three so you can avoid losing sleep over them.

items.t: Hands-on: Counting and Grouping
items.s: The previous four lessons covered the fundamentals. This lesson does the two things dictionaries are **best at**: counting (how many times does each item appear) and grouping (gathering items together under some field).

items.t: Sets: Dedupe, Membership and Disorder
items.s: So far you have met lists, tuples and dictionaries. This lesson introduces the fourth built-in container: **sets**.

items.t: Set Operations: Intersection, Union, Difference, Symmetric Difference
items.s: The most delightful thing about sets is that they ship with the operations you learned in maths class — intersection, union and difference, all in one line.

items.t: Why `in` Is So Fast on a Set
items.s: The last lesson said a set lookup is lightning fast. This lesson will not quote any formulas or talk about big-O; instead it gives you an intuition for **why checking a set is so much faster than checking a list**.

items.t: Choosing Among List, Tuple, Dict and Set
items.s: You have now seen the four built-in containers. The most practical question is: **given a requirement, which one should you pick?**

items.t: Hands-on: Word Frequency Counting
items.s: This is the last "textbook example" in this book — it combines the dictionaries from Chapter 3 with the sets from Chapter 4.

items.t: Why We Need Functions: Stop Copying and Pasting
items.s: Up to now, every program has been one long block of code running from top to bottom. As programs grow, you quickly hit three pains: **repetition**, **hard to change**, and **hard to read**.

items.t: Defining and Calling: def, Parameters, return and Indentation
items.s: The last lesson covered *why* you want functions. This one is about *how* to write one: **how `def` works, how arguments get passed in, what `return` gives back, and what indentation controls**.

items.t: Parameters in Detail: Positional, Default, Keyword, and Order
items.s: The previous lesson showed you *how to write `def`*. This one goes deep on the **parameters**: positional, default, keyword, and **the order they must appear in**.

items.t: Return Values: One, Several, and "Returning Early"
items.s: The previous lesson was about getting values **in**. This one is about handing a result **back**: `return` can give back one value, several values (actually a tuple), end the function early, and how to test for `None`.

items.t: Scope: What Happens Inside Stays Inside
items.s: In earlier lessons we touched on "local variables" in passing. This lesson goes all the way: **where a name is visible, where it is not, and whether a function can change a name from outside.**

items.t: Functions Are Objects: Assign Them, Put Them in Lists, Pass Them In
items.s: So far we have treated a function as "a bundled chunk of code". This lesson upgrades that picture: **a function is itself an object** — you can assign it to a variable, drop it in a list, and pass it as an argument to another function.

items.t: Variable Arguments: `*args` and `**kwargs`
items.s: So far every function has had a fixed number of parameters. This lesson handles "I do not know how many arguments there will be": `*args` gathers any number of **positional arguments**, `**kwargs` gathers any number of **keyword arguments**.

items.t: Lambda and Higher-Order Functions: Tiny One-Line Functions
items.s: This lesson covers "anonymous functions" with `lambda`, plus three of the most useful **higher-order functions**: `map`, `filter` and `sorted(key=...)`.

items.t: Recursion: A Function Calling Itself
items.s: Recursion is "a function that calls itself". It sounds like a tongue-twister, but it is a natural fit for **nested structures that break down into smaller versions of the same problem**.

items.t: Putting It All Together: Refactoring a Mess into Functions
items.s: This is the final lesson of Chapter 6. It uses every technique from the previous five lessons: **take the contacts mini-tool we wrote as "one big lump of code" and reshape it into "a set of functions, each with one job".**

items.t: Why files exist
items.s: Your program forgets everything the moment it closes. This lesson explains why — and what a file actually is.

items.t: open() and the three modes
items.s: Opening a file is one step, but "how you open it" decides what you can do — and what you might destroy.

items.t: Three ways to read
items.s: `read()`, `readline()`, `readlines()` — similar names, completely different behaviour. Pick wrong and you either hang or get the wrong result.

items.t: Writing and newlines
items.s: Reading brings data in; writing sends it out. This lesson covers writing, and the mistake everyone makes.

items.t: Practice: a diary that remembers
items.s: Stringing the first four lessons into something genuinely usable. This is chapter 1's project.

items.t: with: never write close() again
items.s: Forgetting `close()` is the most common file mistake. `with` makes it impossible.

items.t: Paths: relative and absolute
items.s: "File not found" is the most common beginner error. Nine times out of ten it's a path misunderstanding.

items.t: The os module: files and folders
items.s: Beyond reading and writing you need create, delete, rename, list — all in `os`.

items.t: CSV files
items.s: The most widely used format for tabular data. Excel opens it, pandas reads it, Python handles it.

items.t: JSON files
items.s: Need to save a list, a dict, something nested? JSON is the universal answer.

items.t: What an exception is
items.s: Your program doesn't grit its teeth when you make a mistake — it stops and tells you. That stopping-and-telling is an exception.

items.t: try / except: keeping the program alive
items.s: A program that dies at the first error is one nobody dares use. This lesson is about catching them.

items.t: else and finally
items.s: A full `try` has four parts. The last two aren't used every day, but used well they make code much cleaner.

items.t: Raising errors on purpose
items.s: Not just catching — you can create errors too, to refuse inputs that make no sense.

items.t: Practice: a program you can't break
items.s: Use everything from this chapter to write something that survives whatever the user types.

items.t: Why modules exist
items.s: What happens when one file holds 2000 lines? Nothing good. Modules are simply "code split across files".

items.t: Four ways to import
items.s: The same module can be imported several ways. Pick well and your code halves in length.

items.t: Writing your own modules
items.s: You've seen importing others' modules — now write your own, and dodge the "code runs on import" trap.

items.t: Packages: folders of modules
items.s: Once you have many modules, organise them into folders. A folder of modules is a package.

items.t: Tour of the standard library, and pip
items.s: Python ships with hundreds of modules. This lesson covers the ones you'll reach for most, plus installing third-party packages.

items.t: Why classes exist
items.s: Functions package operations, but what about the data? A class packages **data and operations together**.

items.t: Defining classes and creating objects
items.s: You've seen the shape — now every part in detail.

items.t: Class attributes vs instance attributes
items.s: A genuinely confusing point: is the data "one per object" or "one shared by the whole class"?

items.t: Methods and attribute control
items.s: A few techniques that make classes much nicer: `__str__`, default arguments, `property`.

items.t: Practice: a student record system
items.s: Combine classes with file persistence to build something genuinely structured.

items.t: Setup and Your First Program
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will have Python and VSCode installed from scratch and running your very first `hello.py`.

items.t: Variables and Three Kinds of Data
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to store numbers, text, and truth values in variables, and understand how Python classifies them.

items.t: Making Your Program Talk and Listen
items.s: By the end of this lesson your program will be able to "ask a question, wait for an answer, and respond" — it can finally hold a conversation.

items.t: Arithmetic and String Concatenation
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to use Python as a calculator, and understand why the plus sign means two completely different things to numbers and to strings.

items.t: Comments and Reading Error Messages
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to write code that other people can read, and you will stop panicking the first time you see a stack trace — because it is literally telling you which line to fix.

items.t: if / elif / else: teaching your program to decide
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to write "if… otherwise…" logic so your program takes different paths based on input.

items.t: and / or / not and the rules of truthiness
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to combine several conditions, and you will understand what Python considers true and what it considers false.

items.t: while loops: keep going as long as the condition holds
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to write "repeat this while the condition is true" loops, and you will know how to break an infinite loop.

items.t: for and range: when you know how many times
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to control a loop's count precisely with `for`, and you will learn the one rule you must memorise: the endpoint is not included.

items.t: break / continue and nested loops
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to "jump out" of a loop or "skip a round", and you will use nested loops to solve two-dimensional problems.

items.t: Lists: boxes for holding things
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to store a bunch of data in a list, and you will know how to fetch, change, add, remove, and slice it.

items.t: Common list operations
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to sort, concatenate, and count with lists — and you will avoid the trap of "modifying a list while iterating over it", the easiest mistake for a beginner to make.

items.t: Tuples and dictionaries: which to use when
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to tell tuples and lists apart, and you will use dictionaries to look up data by "name".

items.t: Common dictionary operations
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to iterate over dictionaries, safely fetch and delete, and read "a dictionary inside a dictionary" — the real-world data structure.

items.t: Sets: deduplication and set operations
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to deduplicate with sets, compute intersections and unions, and you will know when a set is the right tool for the job.

items.t: Functions: Packaging Code into Reusable Blocks
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to define your own functions with `def` and understand why functions exist in the first place.

items.t: Advanced Parameters: Defaults, Keywords, and `*args`
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to write functions with many optional settings, and you will know the fixed order of positional and keyword arguments.

items.t: Scope: Local and Global Variables
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will know where a variable can be used, where it cannot, and exactly when writing `global` is justified.

items.t: String Methods in Depth
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to split, join, clean, replace, and format strings without writing loops by hand.

items.t: Reading and Writing Files
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to save data to a file and read it back, so your programs finally have a memory.

items.t: Exceptions: try / except / finally
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to make your programs fail gracefully instead of crashing in a wall of red text.

items.t: Modules and Packages: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to use features written by others, and split your own code into reusable modules.

items.t: List Comprehensions and Built-in Functional Tools
items.s: By the end of this lesson you will be able to generate lists in one line, "zip" several sequences together, and use the map / filter / sorted trio for data processing.

items.s: By the end of this lesson you will combine everything from the first 23 lessons into a contact book that can create, read, update, delete, and save to a file.
