items.t: Setting Up Your Environment and Your First Window
items.s: tkinter comes with Python — install Python and you're done. PySide6 needs a separate install, and its windows require an explicit "event loop" to stay alive. This lesson gets your environment ready, opens your first window, and drills the one line people forget: `app.exec()`.

items.t: Why PySide6
items.s: The first decision when learning Qt is which binding to pick: PySide6 or PyQt6. Their APIs are nearly identical — the difference is the license. This lesson lays it out so you don't finish a project and discover you can't ship it commercially.

items.t: Signals and Slots: How They Differ from tkinter's command
items.s: In tkinter, clicking a button calls a function (`command=callback`). That's a "callback". In Qt it's "signals and slots": a widget emits a signal, and you connect it to a slot function. This isn't just a rename — it's a mindset upgrade. One signal can connect to multiple slots; one slot can receive from multiple signals.

items.t: Ways to Write connect
items.s: Lesson 3 covered the concept of signals and slots. This lesson lays out the common ways to write `connect`: connecting built-in signals, connecting custom signals, passing arguments with lambda, and declaring signals with decorators. Once you master custom signals, you've truly grasped Qt's decoupling power.

items.t: Project: A Counter Window
items.s: The first four lessons laid out the concepts. This lesson stitches them together: a counter window where clicking adds 1 and resets to zero. You'll use QVBoxLayout for layout, signals and slots for logic, and QLabel for display — this is what a minimal but complete Qt program looks like.

items.t: Why You Shouldn't Use setGeometry for Layout
items.s: In tkinter you can `btn.place(x=20, y=30)` to set manual coordinates, and in Qt you can `widget.setGeometry(20, 30, 100, 40)`. But this approach is almost never used in real projects. This lesson explains its four flaws and why layout managers are the right choice.

items.t: QVBoxLayout and QHBoxLayout
items.s: Vertical layouts (QVBoxLayout) and horizontal layouts (QHBoxLayout) are Qt's two most commonly used layouts. They're like LEGO bricks: drop widgets in, add stretch factors, set spacing, and your interface comes together. This lesson covers the three core operations: addWidget, addStretch, and setSpacing.

items.t: QGridLayout: Row and Column Grid Layout
items.s: Calculator interfaces, login forms, settings pages — "grid-like" interfaces are best built with QGridLayout. It arranges widgets by row and column, and lets a widget span multiple rows or columns. This lesson covers the parameter order and the most common crash site: wrong parameters causing widgets to pile up.

items.t: QFormLayout and Nested Layouts
items.s: A form interface (label + input appearing in pairs) can be done with QGridLayout, but Qt provides QFormLayout specifically — clearer semantics and automatic wide/narrow screen adaptation. This lesson covers QFormLayout, then layout nesting — combining small layouts into a complete interface.

items.t: Layout Stretching: sizePolicy, setStretch, and minimumSize
items.s: Layouts distribute extra space among widgets, but "who gets it and how much" is governed by the stretch mechanism. This lesson covers three things that control stretching: sizePolicy (the widget's own stated "growth intent"), setStretch (the layout assigning proportions), and minimumSize / maximumSize (size boundaries).

items.t: QLabel, QPushButton, and QLineEdit
items.s: These three are Qt's most basic widgets: QLabel displays text or images, QPushButton triggers actions, and QLineEdit accepts single-line input. You've used them many times already. This lesson fills in their advanced用法 and crash sites.

items.t: QTextEdit and QPlainTextEdit: Multi-Line Text
items.s: Single-line input uses QLineEdit; multi-line uses QTextEdit or QPlainTextEdit. The difference is "do you need rich text?": QTextEdit supports fonts, colors, and images (rich text), while QPlainTextEdit handles only plain text but is faster. This lesson covers how to choose, how to use them, and how to connect the textChanged signal.

items.t: QComboBox, QCheckBox, and QRadioButton
items.s: Dropdown lists, checkboxes, and radio buttons — these are the three workhorses of selection widgets. Their common thread is "pick one or several values", but their interaction differs: dropdowns save space, checkboxes allow multiple selections, and radio buttons enforce a single choice. This lesson covers all three, with emphasis on grouping radio buttons correctly.

items.t: QListWidget and QTableWidget
items.s: Lists and tables are the most common data display formats in any GUI. This lesson covers two "item-based" widgets: QListWidget for one-dimensional lists and QTableWidget for two-dimensional tables. Their APIs are nearly identical — learn one and you'll grasp the other instantly.

items.t: QSlider, QSpinBox, and QProgressBar
items.s: Numeric input and progress feedback are staples of any GUI. QSlider is a draggable slider, QSpinBox is a numeric input box, and QProgressBar is a progress bar — link the three together and you have the classic signal-slot use case.

items.t: QMessageBox: Four Kinds of Prompts and Their Return Values
items.s: Pop-up dialogs are the fastest way to talk to your user. This lesson covers the four standard `QMessageBox` dialogs and how to read which button the user clicked.

items.t: QInputDialog / QFileDialog / QColorDialog
items.s: Three built-in dialogs you'll use constantly: grab a value, pick a file, choose a color. Each is a one-liner static method — but they all hide the same trap: the user might cancel.

items.t: Custom Dialogs with QDialog
items.s: Built-in dialogs can only fetch a single value. A real interaction needs its own layout. This lesson shows how to build a `QDialog` — and why `exec()` can return a value while `show()` cannot.

items.t: QMenuBar / QToolBar / QStatusBar
items.s: Menus, toolbars, and status bars are the "front-door trio" of a desktop app. This lesson covers how to write each one and how they work together.

items.t: QAction: Define Once, Mount Anywhere
items.s: A `QAction` is an "action" object: one logical operation that can live in both a menu and a toolbar, complete with icon and shortcut. It is the shared atom of menus and toolbars.

items.t: Getting Started with QSS
items.s: Qt Style Sheets (QSS) are Qt's styling language. The syntax is so close to CSS it's almost identical. This lesson shows how to beautify an interface with QSS — and exactly where it differs from CSS.

items.t: Common QSS Patterns
items.s: This lesson works through the QSS patterns you'll reach for constantly: button hover/press, borders and corners, and input focus. Learn these templates and you can style most interfaces.

items.t: The Resource System: qrc
items.s: Bundling images into your program means you don't ship a folder full of loose files. This lesson covers the `qrc` resource file and the `pyrcc6` compilation flow.

items.t: Icons and Fonts
items.s: Icons should be sharp and fonts should look good — and both should stay crisp on a 4K screen. This lesson covers `QIcon`'s multi-resolution mechanism, font settings, and DPI handling.

items.t: Dark Mode and Theme Switching
items.s: A "switch theme" button is really just dynamically replacing a QSS string. This lesson covers how to organize two themes and the easiest traps to fall into when switching.

items.t: Why You Must Not Do Heavy Work in the GUI
items.s: The most damaging mistake in a GUI app is not a crash — it is "freezing". This lesson explains how the main-thread blocking actually works and which jobs belong elsewhere.

items.t: QThread and the Worker Pattern
items.s: Move the heavy work to a background thread so the interface is always smooth. This lesson covers the correct use of `QThread` — and the one landmine everyone steps on.

items.t: QTimer: The Right Way to Schedule Work
items.s: `QTimer` lets you schedule tasks without ever freezing the interface. This lesson explains how `QTimer` works — and why `time.sleep` is poison in a GUI.

items.t: Project: Batch File Renamer
items.s: Lessons 14, 15, 17, and 27 come together in one project — multi-threading, progress bars, file dialogs, and tables — to build a tool that actually does something useful.

items.t: Wrapping Up: Project Organization and What's Next
items.s: Twenty-five lessons are done. This final lesson covers how to organize a Qt project, how to package it for distribution, and what awaits in *Python Qt 进阶 2*.

items.t: Why Model/View Exists: QTableWidget Works Fine Until It Doesn't
items.s: You built a 100-row table with QTableWidget and it felt great. Then product asks for "10,000 rows, live sorting, keyword filtering" and your code collapses.

items.t: Model and View Responsibilities: QAbstractItemModel, QTableView, index, row, and column
items.s: Last lesson you were sold on Model/View. This lesson takes it apart: the model is the data's "interface," the view is the data's "mouthpiece," and they communicate through a protocol. The model never knows about any widget.

items.t: Getting Started with QStandardItemModel: The Go-To Ready-Made Model
items.s: Don't want to write a custom model but need Model/View flexibility? QStandardItemModel is Qt's "half-sugar" solution: a built-in data container you can use right away — get the pipeline running first, customize later.

items.t: Custom Models: Subclassing QAbstractTableModel and the Three Methods You Must Implement
items.s: QStandardItemModel is enough — until your data lives in a CSV, a database, or a network API. Then you write your own model: tell Qt how many rows, how many columns, and what each cell contains.

items.t: Data Change Notifications: beginInsertRows/endInsertRows — Modifying the Internal List Without Notifying Means No Refresh (The Classic Trap)
items.s: This is the most core and most easily overlooked lesson in Model/View. Previous lessons' signals were "automatic." This lesson covers the notifications you must send manually: telling the view "I'm about to insert a row" and "I just finished deleting a row." Skip them and you have a bug.

items.t: QSortFilterProxyModel: Sorting and Filtering Without Touching Your Data
items.s: You built a solid model. Now the product manager comes back: it needs sorting, and a search box. You do not change a single line of the model — you drop a `QSortFilterProxyModel` in between, and the original data stays completely untouched.

items.t: Custom Sorting and Filtering: lessThan and filterAcceptsRow
items.s: Default string sorting is not enough. You want "Pending < In Progress < Done", or sorting by date, or showing only rows "where the amount is over 1000 and the status is not Done". For these you must write your own logic — subclass the proxy and override `lessThan` and `filterAcceptsRow`.

items.t: Delegates: Why Cells Need to Show Buttons, Progress Bars, and Dropdowns
items.s: Must a cell contain only text? No. Delegates are the third piece of the Model/View puzzle: they decide how a cell is drawn and how it is edited. The default `QStyledItemDelegate` draws text and pops up a plain input box; if you want a progress bar, a dropdown, or a button, you must write your own delegate.

items.t: Custom Delegates: paint and createEditor, plus setEditorData and setModelData
items.s: Lesson 08 covered `paint`, so a cell can now look different. This lesson makes it editable: double-click to pop up a calendar, a dropdown, or a star selector. The key is how the four methods cooperate — miss one and the edit simply does not work.

items.t: Selection Models: QItemSelectionModel for Tracking and Reacting to Selection
items.s: The user clicked a row — how do you know? A view's selection state is actually owned by a dedicated class: `QItemSelectionModel`. It answers three questions: "which index is current?", "which rows are selected?", and "who should be told when the selection changes?"

items.t: Why Custom Widgets: When Stock Widgets Cannot Build the Look You Need
items.s: `QPushButton`, `QLabel`, `QProgressBar` are already excellent. But sooner or later the PM points at a design and says: "I want this rounded, gradient-filled button with a ripple on click." That is when you discover that snapping widgets together cannot get you there.

items.t: Subclassing Existing Widgets: Extending QPushButton with a Countdown and a Custom Signal
items.s: Full custom painting is heavy, and QSS is not enough. This lesson covers "subclassing an existing widget": inherit all of the parent's behaviour and add only the small piece you need — a countdown, a custom signal, an extra property. This is the highest-leverage form of customisation.

items.t: Full Custom Painting: Subclassing QWidget and Painting Only Inside paintEvent
items.s: Subclassing got you 90% there, but the shape you need does not exist as a widget — ring progress, waveform, dashboard. Now you go all the way: subclass `QWidget` and paint it yourself with `QPainter`. The one rule that cannot be broken is that the painting happens inside `paintEvent`.

items.t: Event Handling: mousePressEvent and keyPressEvent, and the Difference Between event and eventFilter
items.s: A hand-painted widget does not respond to clicks by itself — you handle mouse and keyboard events yourself. This lesson covers the event dispatch mechanism and the difference between `event()` and event filters.

items.t: Custom Widgets in Practice: A Circular Progress Indicator
items.s: Every tool from the previous three lessons comes together: a hand-painted widget subclassing `QWidget`, mouse events, custom signals, and `QTimer` for animation. The result is a circular progress indicator you can click, animate, and signal from.

items.t: Getting Started with QPainter
items.s: Want to draw a line, a circle, or a piece of text on a window? In PySide6 every custom paint operation comes back to one class — `QPainter` — and it has exactly one valid home: `paintEvent`.

items.t: Basic Shapes: Lines, Rectangles, Circles, Polygons, Text, and Images
items.s: Last section you drew a line. This section opens up the full "shape toolbox": straight lines, rectangles, rounded rectangles, ellipses, polygons, text, and images — plus the one switch that makes everything look polished: antialiasing.

items.t: Coordinate Transforms: translate, rotate, scale, and the State Stack
items.s: Want to draw a needle that rotates around its center, a repeating pattern, or a fractal that scales to any size? Computing coordinates by hand is painful. `QPainter`'s built-in coordinate transforms plus a state stack let you manipulate a "local canvas" however you like.

items.t: Gradients and Paths: QLinearGradient / QRadialGradient and QPainterPath
items.s: Solid fills are everywhere; gradients are what give a control its sense of depth. And `QPainterPath` lets you draw any arbitrary outline — rounded tags, arrows, progress arcs, irregular buttons — all of it.

items.t: Hands-On: A Custom Gauge Control
items.s: Now we tie together everything from the last four sections — paintEvent, shapes, coordinate transforms, gradients, and paths. In this section we build a reusable circular gauge: tick marks, tick labels, a colored arc, a needle, a value readout — all painted inside one QWidget.

items.t: Database Support in Qt: The QtSql Module and QSqlTableModel
items.s: Qt ships with its own database module, `QtSql` — no need to install SQLAlchemy to talk to SQLite, MySQL, or PostgreSQL. Even better, it integrates with the Model/View architecture out of the box: bind a table directly to a `QTableView` and it's editable immediately.

items.t: QSqlQuery and Hand-Written SQL: Parameterized Queries, Iterating Results, and Transactions
items.s: When you need joins, aggregation, or complex conditions, a Model isn't enough. `QSqlQuery` lets you write SQL directly — but you must follow two iron rules: **always parameterize, and always check the exec return value.**

items.t: QtSql Meets Model/View: QSqlQueryModel vs QSqlTableModel
items.s: Both "bind a SQL result to a QTableView" — yet `QSqlQueryModel` and `QSqlTableModel` take two different paths: one is read-only for arbitrary SELECTs, the other is editable for a single table. This section unpacks that choice.

items.t: QNetworkAccessManager Basics: Asynchronous HTTP Requests and Responses
items.s: A desktop app that fetches data from the network could use `requests`, but that's synchronous — call it and the UI freezes. Qt's approach is asynchronous: `QNetworkAccessManager` sends the request, and a signal delivers the response when it arrives.

items.t: JSON and Network Data: Parsing API Responses and Feeding Them into a Model
items.s: The end goal of a network request is usually a JSON payload. This section connects the full chain — "network request -> JSON parsing -> into a Model -> bound to a View" — to build a genuine "online data table."

items.t: Project Design: Rewriting the tkinter Ledger with Qt
items.s: This volume has taken you from Model/View to drawing to networking. The capstone project is to **rewrite the tkinter ledger app you built in "Window Basics 3" entirely in Qt** — same database, completely different UI layer.

items.t: The Data Layer and the Model: Turning Database Rows into Qt Data
items.s: The previous lesson settled the layering. This lesson does the actual work: write a `TransactionModel` that turns the result of an SQLite query into something a `QAbstractTableModel` can hand back to a view. The data layer stays exactly what it was — the Model is the translator.

items.t: The Interface and Interaction: Sorting, Filtering, Entry and Delete
items.s: The model is ready. This lesson wires it up to a view. The two key pieces are `QSortFilterProxyModel` for sorting and category filtering, and `QItemSelectionModel` for "select and delete".

items.t: Hand-Drawn Charts: Pie and Bar Charts with QPainter
items.s: Chapter 4's drawing skills finally have real work to do. This lesson uses `QPainter` to draw a category-share pie chart and a monthly-trend bar chart — turning "I can draw" into "I can draw something meaningful".

items.t: Wrapping Up: Packaging for Release and What Two Volumes Leave You With
items.s: The project is finished. Two things remain: turn it into an executable you can hand to someone, and look back at what these two volumes have actually given you.

items.t: Why Data Formats Matter
items.s: This lesson answers a simple question: how do two programs hand data to each other intact? You will understand that `print` output is for human eyes, while `json.dumps` output is for programs.

items.t: `dumps` and `loads`: Four Functions, Two Pairs
items.s: This lesson thoroughly covers the four most commonly used functions in the `json` module. You only need to remember two pairs: use `dumps`/`loads` for **strings**, and `dump`/`load` for **files**.

items.t: The Type Mapping Table: What Converts and What Crashes
items.s: This lesson explains the type conversion rules between Python and JSON. If you do not memorize them, you will get bugs: `(1, 2)` goes in and comes back as `[1, 2]`.

items.t: Reading and Writing Files: `dump`, `load`, and Three Key Parameters
items.s: This lesson covers how to actually store JSON on disk and read it back. You will learn the three parameters that make files "both usable and readable": `ensure_ascii`, `indent`, and `sort_keys`.

items.t: Chinese Characters and Encoding: Why Files Become Garbled
items.s: This lesson explains exactly why "reading and writing files produces garbled text." You will never again say "I just opened it casually" without being able to pinpoint whether the problem lies with UTF-8, GBK, or the BOM.

items.t: Accessing Nested Structures: Safe Retrieval from Multi-Level Dicts and Lists
items.s: This lesson answers: "After reading JSON, how do you safely retrieve values from deep within?" You will learn chained `get` access to prevent a `KeyError` from crashing your entire script.

items.t: Custom Object Serialization: `default` and `object_hook`
items.s: This lesson answers: "How do I store my class objects in JSON?" Building on the pitfalls from Lesson 03, you will learn to use `default=` to convert arbitrary objects into JSON and `object_hook` to restore them.

items.t: `JSONDecodeError`: Common Bad JSON and Locating Errors
items.s: This lesson is dedicated to the question: "What do I do when parsing fails?" You will learn to read the line and column numbers in error messages and recognize the most common JSON mistakes.

items.t: When JSON Is Not Enough
items.s: This lesson gives you a "boundary checklist": dates, binary data, circular references, tuples/sets — JSON cannot represent these. Learning to recognize them tells you when it is time to switch approaches.

items.t: Hands-On: A Configuration Read/Write Module
items.s: This lesson ties together everything from Chapter 2: reading config, modifying config, writing it back to a file, with defaults and fault tolerance. When you are done, you will have a `config.py` that you can use directly in your own projects.

items.t: The `csv` Module and Why You Cannot Just `split(',')`
items.s: This lesson tells you: CSV looks simple, but commas inside quotes and newlines inside fields will make your hand-written parser collapse completely. Python's standard `csv` module was built for exactly these pitfalls.

items.t: `reader` / `writer`: Reading and Writing in List Form
items.s: This lesson dives into `csv.reader` and `csv.writer`: how to read, how to write, and what the return types are. It also thoroughly explains why `newline=''` is mandatory.

items.t: `DictReader` / `DictWriter`: Reading and Writing by Column Name
items.s: The previous lesson used index-based column access (`row[0]`, `row[1]`), which is fragile — any change to the header breaks everything. This lesson replaces indices with column names, making your code more robust and readable.

items.t: CSV Encoding and Dialect Pitfalls
items.s: This lesson tackles "why it is all garbled when you open it" and "why are the delimiters wrong." The differences between UTF-8 and GBK, how to change the delimiter, and the four quoting strategies — they are all here.

items.t: Hands-On: A CSV ↔ JSON Conversion Utility
items.s: This lesson ties together everything from Chapter 3 by building a conversion utility you can use from the command line. The focus is on **type restoration** — since CSV contains only strings, you must restore them to numbers, booleans, and null when converting to JSON.

items.t: configparser: How to Read INI Configuration Files
items.s: This lesson solves "how to read configuration when your program starts." You no longer need to write a custom `key=value` parser — the standard library ships one called `configparser`. By the end, you'll understand: **everything it returns is a string**, which is where newcomers trip up most often.

items.t: pickle: Serialising Arbitrary Python Objects to Bytes
items.s: This lesson solves "how to store things that JSON can't." Custom class instances, structures with circular references, sets, complex numbers — `pickle` handles all of them. The cost is that what it produces can only be read by Python.

items.t: pickle Security Warning: Never Unpickle Untrusted Data
items.s: This lesson covers exactly one thing, but it's the most critical security red line in the entire standard library: **if you can construct a pickle byte string, you can execute arbitrary code on the machine doing the deserialisation.** Don't believe it? This lesson demonstrates it live.

items.t: base64: Slipping Binary Data into Text-Only Contexts
items.s: This lesson solves "how to embed images, signatures, or archives into JSON / email / URLs." Binary bytes can't be placed raw into text protocols — base64 is that translation layer, turning 3 bytes into 4 printable characters.

items.t: hashlib: Verifying Data Integrity — and Why Passwords Must Never Be Stored in Plain Text
items.s: This lesson tackles two closely related problems: whether a downloaded file has been tampered with (data integrity), and how your password database should be structured (**plain text is never acceptable**). Both use "hash algorithms," but for entirely different purposes.

items.t: decimal: Why £0.1 + £0.2 Does Not Equal £0.3
items.s: This lesson settles, once and for all, the question of "why you must never use float for money." You'll see the `0.1 + 0.2` trap for yourself, and learn to do it right with `decimal.Decimal` — **construct with strings, never floats.**

items.t: fractions: Exact Computation with Fractions, Avoiding Float Error
items.s: When a business deals in "ratios," "recipes," or "allocations," floats drift further off the mark with every calculation. This lesson gets you fluent with `fractions.Fraction` and spells out the pitfall of mixing it with floats.

items.t: dataclasses: Cutting Your Boilerplate by 80%
items.s: A class that just holds data needs an `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`... Write it three times and you'll be sick of it. This lesson uses `@dataclass` to generate them automatically, so you can focus on the fields themselves.

items.t: enum: Killing Magic Strings with Enumerations
items.s: Is your code full of `"pending"`, `"paid"`, `"shipped"`? This lesson gathers them into a named, typed enum class — never misspell one again.

items.t: In Practice: An Order Data Validator
items.s: This is the capstone project of chapter 5. We'll stitch `decimal`, `enum`, `dataclasses`, and `json` together into a complete order-validation system that can read, validate, and report.

items.t: Lesson 26 · The Data Pipeline Toolkit: Project Design
items.s: Putting every tool from the first 25 lessons into one real project — a command-line data pipeline that actually runs.

items.t: Lesson 27 · The Data Pipeline: Reading Multiple Formats
items.s: The load layer's goal — no matter what format arrives, out comes `list[dict]`.

items.t: Lesson 28 · The Data Pipeline: Cleaning and Validation
items.s: The core principle of validation — **collect every error, not just the first one.**

items.t: Lesson 29 · The Data Pipeline: Output and Logging
items.s: The dump layer writes the cleaned data out; logging tells developers what happened inside the program.

items.t: Lesson 30 · The Grand Finale: Assembling the CLI Tool + Book Recap
items.s: Connecting all four layers into a runnable command-line tool. Then looking back at what you're taking away from this book.

items.t: Why Time Is Hard
items.s: This lesson answers "why time is one of the trickiest data types in programming." You will see why hand-rolling date math is a bad idea, and how deep the pitfalls of time zones, leap seconds, and daylight saving time really go.

items.t: The Three Siblings: date, time, datetime
items.s: This lesson answers "which of `date`, `time`, or `datetime` should I actually use?" You will learn what each type covers, and when to combine them versus when to keep them separate.

items.t: timedelta: Time Deltas and Date Arithmetic
items.s: This lesson answers "how do I correctly add days to a date, or find how far apart two moments are?" You will also learn the boundaries of `timedelta` — it handles days and seconds, but **not months**.

items.t: Formatting: strftime and strptime
items.s: This lesson answers "how do I turn a date object into a string for a human, and a string back into a date object?" You will memorise the most useful placeholders, and learn why `%` must be escaped inside a format string.

items.t: Timestamps
items.s: This lesson answers "why should I pass time as a timestamp when talking between systems, and what are the time-zone traps when converting to and from a timestamp?" You will see why storing local time directly can cause bugs.

items.t: Time Zones: naive vs aware
items.s: This lesson answers "why can't I mix zoned and unzoned times, and how do I work with time zones properly using zoneinfo?" You will learn the golden rule: store UTC, display local.

items.t: Timing: perf_counter vs time.time
items.s: This lesson answers "how do I measure how long my code takes to run?" You will learn why `time.time()` is the wrong tool for timing, and why `perf_counter` is the right one.

items.t: Advanced Date Arithmetic
items.s: This lesson answers "what is the last day of the month, which ISO week does a date fall in, and how do I count working days?" You will use the `calendar` module and built-in date methods to handle these everyday requirements.

items.t: Parsing Dates in the Wild
items.s: This lesson answers "users type dates in every format imaginable — how do I parse them forgivingly?" You will learn to try multiple formats with try/except, and discover the limits of format-based parsing.

items.t: Capstone: A Countdown and Schedule Tool
items.s: This lesson ties the first nine lessons together into a usable "event countdown" tool. You will see how to combine `date`, `timedelta`, and `strftime` to solve a real problem.

items.t: os.path vs pathlib
items.s: This lesson answers "how do I represent file paths in Python?" You will see why `pathlib` beats string concatenation, and the traps that catch even experienced developers using `os.path`.

items.t: Working with Paths in pathlib
items.s: This lesson takes the common operations of `pathlib` apart in detail. You will learn to join paths with `/`, pull the pieces apart, check what exists, and create directories — all through `Path` methods.

items.t: Walking Directories
items.s: This lesson shows how to dig files out of a directory tree — from the one-level-at-a-time `iterdir()`, through pattern matching with `glob()`, to the deep traversal of `os.walk()`. You will learn to filter by name, find files recursively, and understand the subtle difference between `*` and `**`.

items.t: File Metadata
items.s: This lesson covers how to read a file's size, modification time, and other metadata, and how to turn a Unix timestamp into a human-readable datetime. You will learn how to use `stat()`, and understand the relationship between `os.path.getsize` and `Path.stat().st_size`.

items.t: Capstone: A Batch-Rename Tool
items.s: This lesson brings everything you have learned about `pathlib` together into a command-line batch-rename tool. Its core design principle is: **preview first, then apply** — never silently renaming files. You will also handle name collisions and build an undo mechanism.

items.t: Reading and Writing Files the Right Way
items.s: This lesson answers one question: how do you read and write files safely? You will understand why `with` is mandatory, how the four modes `r / w / a / x` differ, and which trade-offs matter when choosing between `read`, `readline`, `readlines`, and line iteration.

items.t: High-Level File Operations with shutil
items.s: The `os` module handles one file at a time. Moving across filesystems and copying entire directory trees require `shutil`. This lesson covers the differences between `copy`, `copy2`, `move`, `rmtree`, and `copytree`, and identifies the single most dangerous call in the module.

items.t: Temporary Files and Directories
items.s: This lesson explains why you should never write `open("/tmp/scratch", "w")` yourself: concurrent collisions, permission leaks, and forgotten cleanup are all waiting. You will learn `TemporaryFile`, `NamedTemporaryFile`, `mkdtemp`, and the classic `delete` trap.

items.t: The os Module and System Information
items.s: This lesson shows how to read environment variables, detect the current operating system, and run system commands from Python. You will learn the correct use of `os.environ` and understand why `os.system` has been replaced by `subprocess`.

items.t: The subprocess Module Basics
items.s: This lesson shows how to invoke external commands safely from Python. The core is `subprocess.run()`: `capture_output` collects output, `check=True` turns failures into exceptions, and one rule is non-negotiable—**never pass user input to `shell=True`.**

items.t: zipfile: Creating and Reading Zip Archives
items.s: This lesson covers Python's `zipfile` module. You will learn to create zips, list their contents, read individual files, extract them, and understand the practical limits of password protection.

items.t: tarfile: Choosing Between tar.gz, tar.bz2, and tar.xz
items.s: This lesson covers Python's `tarfile` module and the differences between `.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, and `.tar.xz`. You will learn how to choose the right compression format for each situation.

items.t: To Compress or Not to Compress
items.s: This lesson covers a counterintuitive fact: many common files cannot be compressed further. You will see which formats are already compressed, which still have room, and what compression ratios are realistic.

items.t: glob and fnmatch: Filename Pattern Matching
items.s: This lesson presents a pair of modules: `fnmatch` tests whether a single filename matches a shell-style pattern, while `glob` expands that pattern into a real file list. You will learn their syntax and how each one relates to `pathlib.glob`.

items.t: Project: A Backup Tool
items.s: This lesson brings Chapters 4 and 5 together: traverse a directory with `pathlib`, filter exclusions with `fnmatch`, package archives with `tarfile` or `zipfile`, name them with timestamps, and simulate checksums. You will build a usable command-line backup tool.

items.t: Project Design: A Smart File Organiser
items.s: The previous five chapters gave you a toolbox of parts—time, paths, files, and archives. This chapter assembles them into one machine: a tool that actually organises your download folder.

items.t: Scanning and Classification: Turning a Directory into Data
items.s: Building on `pathlib` traversal from Chapter 3, this lesson turns "scanning a directory" into a data pipeline: skip what should be skipped, collect what matters, and emit a clean file list.

items.t: The Rule Engine: Configurable Classification and Date-Based Archiving
items.s: Hardcoding classification rules makes a toy. This lesson turns rules into data and adds date-based archiving—putting the time knowledge from Chapters 1 and 2 to work.

items.t: Execution and Undo: Making the Tool Trustworthy
items.s: Generating a plan is only paper. Moving files is where the value—and the risk—appears. This lesson explains why undo is the dividing line between a professional tool and a throwaway script.

items.t: The Final Assembly: A Runnable Tool and a Path to Standard Library 3
items.s: The previous four lessons produced the parts. This lesson wires them into a command-line program with progress feedback and exception handling—then looks back at everything this book has given you.

items.t: Why Regular Expressions Exist
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I pull out the small piece I want from a messy blob of text?" You'll see why `split` and `find` become unbearable, and how one regex can express "find a phone number" in a single line.

items.t: Basic Matching: search, match, and findall
items.s: This lesson answers: "Which key opens which lock?" `re.search`, `re.match`, and `re.fullmatch` look nearly identical, but they are three completely different search postures. `findall` and `finditer` each have their own strengths too.

items.t: Character Classes and Quantifiers
items.s: This lesson answers: "How do I describe a whole category of characters, or a length, in one sentence?" `.`, `\d`, `\w`, `\s` are shorthands; `[]`, `*`, `+`, `?`, `{m,n}` are quantifiers—and their combination is where regex gets its real expressive power. **Greedy vs. non-greedy** is the most valuable trap in this lesson.

items.t: Groups and Capturing
items.s: This lesson answers: "I matched it, but I only want to take out part of it." `()` for capturing, `(?:)` for non-capturing, `(?P<name>)` for named groups—and the **single most classic regex trap**: `findall` returns only the groups when groups are present.

items.t: Replacement and Splitting: sub and split
items.s: This lesson covers two things: "change what you matched into something else" and "cut by a pattern." `re.sub` can use a string, a function, or group references. `re.split` can cut on irregular delimiters like "one or more spaces."

items.t: Compiling Regex: re.compile and Flags
items.s: This lesson answers: "How do I handle performance and readability when I use the same pattern many times?" `re.compile` precompiles a pattern into an object. `IGNORECASE`, `MULTILINE`, and `DOTALL` each solve one specific pain point.

items.t: Common Real-World Patterns: Email, Phone, IP, Date, URL
items.s: This lesson stitches the syntax you've learned into ready-to-use patterns you can copy. It also makes a more important point: **don't chase the perfect regex**—good enough is good enough; boundary cases belong to business rules.

items.t: Regex Performance: Catastrophic Backtracking
items.s: This lesson answers: "Why does my regex hang?" Some seemingly harmless patterns, when faced with "almost matching" input, cause the engine to backtrack exponentially—and bring down a service. Learning to recognize nested quantifiers is regex's rite of passage.

items.t: When Not to Use Regex
items.s: This lesson is about **knowing when to stop**. Regex isn't a silver bullet: it loses to dedicated tools for structured text, and for simple splitting, string methods are faster and more readable. Learning to judge "this isn't worth a regex" is more valuable than learning more regex syntax.

items.t: Real-World Project: A Log Parser
items.s: This lesson turns the first 9 regex lessons into something usable: a log parser. The input is a pile of log lines; the output is structured records of "time, level, message," plus a count by level. This is regex's most typical and most realistic application.

items.t: collections.Counter: Counting Made Effortless
items.s: This lesson answers: "How do I count things?" A hand-written dictionary counter takes 4 lines and is easy to get wrong; `Counter` does it in one, and can even tell you "who's winning."

items.t: defaultdict and OrderedDict
items.s: This lesson answers: "How do I handle nested dict-of-list or dict-of-dict structures cleanly?" `defaultdict` lets you append without checking for the key first. `OrderedDict` preserves insertion order—but since Python 3.7+, plain `dict` is already ordered, so it now has only niche uses.

items.t: collections.deque: Double-Ended Queue
items.s: This lesson answers: "What about queues that operate at both ends?" `list.pop(0)` is an O(n) hidden performance killer; `deque.popleft()` is O(1). Understanding the cost difference is the prerequisite for writing a high-performance circular queue.

items.t: itertools Essentials: chain, product, combinations, permutations, groupby
items.s: This lesson covers the five most-used `itertools` tools in one pass. They're all **lazy iterators**—memory-efficient and composable. The focus is `groupby`: **it must be pre-sorted first**, which is its nastiest trap.

items.t: functools: Caching, Partial Application, and Reduction
items.s: This lesson covers the three most practical tools in `functools`: `lru_cache` cuts repeated computation to O(1); `partial` turns "binding arguments" into a new function; `reduce` folds a stream of values into one. Together they're core parts of writing in a functional style.

items.t: Logging Basics: Stop Debugging with `print`
items.s: This lesson answers "why isn't `print` good enough?" and covers the five logging levels plus the correct use of `basicConfig`. Think of `print` as a sticky note you scribble on; `logging` is a proper system with severity, timestamps, and an on/off switch.

items.t: Logging In Depth: Loggers, Handlers, and Formatters
items.s: This lesson lays out the internal architecture of the logging system: a logger decides what to emit, a handler decides where it goes, and a formatter decides how it looks. Plus two classic traps — never call `basicConfig` in every module, and beware of duplicate output.

items.t: Logging in Practice: What Developers Need vs. What Users Need
items.s: This lesson covers the two audiences for log output: developers want detailed exception traces and context; users want one plain sentence. It also covers logging exceptions with `exc_info` and rotating files by date.

items.t: argparse Basics: Parsing Command-Line Arguments Properly
items.s: This lesson covers the basic usage of `argparse`: positional arguments, optional arguments, `type`, `default`, `help`, and validating input with `choices`. The days of hand-rolling `sys.argv` parsing are over.

items.t: argparse In Depth: Subcommands and Mutually Exclusive Groups
items.s: This lesson covers advanced `argparse` usage: organising subcommands the way `git clone` and `git push` do, using mutually exclusive groups to prevent conflicting arguments, and comparing the result with hand-rolled `sys.argv` parsing.

items.t: Why Tests Matter
items.s: This lesson covers the need for tests: you change one line and have no idea what else broke, and clicking through manually is slow. Tests are insurance for your code — a small price for a large saving.

items.t: unittest Basics: Writing Tests with a Framework
items.s: This lesson covers Python's standard-library testing framework, `unittest`: TestCase, assertEqual/assertTrue/assertRaises, plus setUp/tearDown and how to run tests.

items.t: Test Organisation: One Function Per Test, Boundary Values, Repeatability
items.s: This lesson covers how to organise tests so they're reliable: one test verifies one thing, covers boundary values (empty, single, huge), and produces stable, repeatable results — no leaning on randomness or the current time.

items.t: Introducing pytest: Why So Many People Use It
items.s: This lesson covers pytest's core strengths: a far simpler assertion syntax and the fixture mechanism. It also explains how pytest relates to unittest. No installation required — this is concepts and comparison only.

items.t: Hands-On: Writing a Complete Test Suite for a Small Module
items.s: This lesson brings everything together: building a real small module (a shopping cart), writing a full set of unit tests, running them, and then deliberately introducing bugs to see whether the tests catch them.

items.t: Project Design: A Log Analysis CLI Tool
items.s: This lesson starts building something genuinely "showcase-worthy" — combining the first 25 lessons into a complete project: a log analysis tool that runs on the command line.

items.t: The Parsing Layer: Regex Extraction with Fault Tolerance
items.s: This lesson applies the regex knowledge from Chapters 1 and 2 to a real scenario — extracting structured information from log text while ensuring that dirty data never brings the tool down.

items.t: The Statistics Layer: Multi-Dimensional Aggregation
items.s: This lesson uses Counter / defaultdict / itertools from Chapter 3 to run multi-dimensional statistics over the parsed logs — level distribution, time distribution, top N errors, and per-module rankings.

items.t: The Output Layer: Multiple Formats and Tool Logging
items.s: This lesson makes statistics visible and storable — console tables, JSON export, and CSV export working together, plus using logging to record the tool's own runtime activity.

items.t: Finale: Assembling the CLI and What the Three Books Leave You With
items.s: The final lesson wires the parsing, statistics, and output layers into a complete CLI tool using argparse subcommands, tests it with unittest, and then looks back at what these three books have actually given you — including a roadmap for where to go next.

items.t: What the Browser, HTML and CSS Each Do
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How does the text I write become a web page?" Understanding the division of labour makes it obvious where to look when something goes wrong.

items.t: Your First HTML Document: Get the Skeleton Right
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Why does my page look odd in the browser?" The root cause is the skeleton: doctype, html, head and body - not one of them can be missing.

items.t: Headings and Paragraphs: The Semantics of h1-h6
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Which tag should I use for a heading?" The key idea is: **h1 means "this is a level-one heading", not "this is large text".**

items.t: Text Tags: strong, em, span and div
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I add emphasis to a piece of text?" There is only one test: **do you want to express meaning, or do you want to express a look?**

items.t: Attributes and Links: href, target and alt
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I write those extra pieces of information on a tag?" Attributes are the "parameters" of a tag; links and images cannot do without them.

items.t: Three Ways to Write CSS
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Where does CSS go?" All three ways work, but their maintenance costs are very different.

items.t: Selectors: Tag, Class and id
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Exactly which elements will my styles apply to?" Pick accurately and your styles stay maintainable.

items.t: Colours and Units
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I write a colour, and which unit should I use for sizes?" Picking the right unit lets your page adapt across different screens.

items.t: The Box Model: Every Element Is a Box
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Why is the width I set not the width I see?" The box model is the most fundamental - and most easily mishandled - part of CSS.

items.t: Text Styling: Fonts, Line Height and Alignment
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Why does my text look bad?" Font size, line height and letter spacing are the properties that decide how readable your page is.

items.t: Lists: ul, ol and dl
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I organise a group of parallel items?" Why does a navigation menu use a list? Because it already is "a set of parallel options".

items.t: Tables: table, tr, td and th
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I present data laid out in rows and columns?" A table should be used only for tabular data, never for page layout.

items.t: Images: img's src, alt, width and height
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Why is my image not showing, and why does the page jump?" Path and size are the two most common image problems.

items.t: Semantic Tags: header, nav, main, section, article and footer
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "My page is nothing but divs, and machines cannot tell what it is about." Semantic tags let the structure speak for itself.

items.t: Forms Basics: form, input, label, button, textarea and select
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I let a user enter information and submit it?" The focus is on how a label is associated - it decides whether every user can click and fill in the form easily.

items.t: display: the three states of block, inline and inline-block
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Why do some elements take up a whole line while others sit side by side and refuse to accept a width?" `display` decides how an element exists in the normal flow, and it is the starting point for every layout you will ever build.

items.t: float and clearing floats: the normal flow, bypassed
items.s: This lesson answers two questions: "How do I wrap text around a picture?" and "Why did two divs sitting side by side collapse their parent container?" `float` carries a lot of historical baggage. Once you understand it you will see why Flex is the preferred choice today.

items.t: position: putting elements exactly where you want them
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I pin an element precisely at a certain place on the page?" There are five values for `position`. The classic combination is `relative` for the reference and `absolute` for the placement.

items.t: Flex basics: one-dimensional layout with flexbox
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I space a few elements evenly along the main axis?" Flex is the workhorse of modern layout — one line of CSS replaces the whole pile of floats and clearfixes you used to need.

items.t: Flex further: direction, wrapping and flexible distribution
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I make Flex items stack vertically, wrap onto a new line or share space by ratio?" `flex-direction`, `flex-wrap` and `flex` cover almost every everyday layout need.

items.t: Why responsive design matters
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How can one codebase look good on both a phone and a desktop?" Responsive is not a bonus feature — in 2026 it is a baseline requirement. Mobile traffic is already the mainstream.

items.t: The viewport and media queries
items.s: This lesson answers two questions: "Why does my page shrink into a thumbnail on a phone?" and "How do I write different CSS for different screens?"

items.t: Relative units and fluid layout
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Why shouldn't I hard-code widths?" and "How do I choose between rem, em, %, and vw?" Pick the right unit and your layout flows with the screen.

items.t: Grid basics: the two-dimensional grid system
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I control rows and columns at the same time?" Flex is one-dimensional (it handles one row or one column at a time); Grid is two-dimensional (rows and columns together). They complement each other rather than replace each other.

items.t: Transitions and animations: bring the page to life
items.s: This lesson answers two questions: "How do I make a button change colour smoothly on hover?" and "How do I build a loading animation?" CSS animations need no JavaScript, and the browser accelerates them on the GPU for great performance.

items.t: Project design: planning a personal CV page
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Where do I start when I am given a page requirement?" A good front-end developer does not open the editor and start writing `<div>` straight away — they think through the structure, the colour scheme and the information hierarchy first.

items.t: Building the HTML skeleton: semantic tags for the CV
items.s: This lesson turns the design from the previous lesson into HTML. The focus is **picking the right tag** — give every region the tag that fits it best, so the structure itself becomes the document.

items.t: Writing the CSS: a proto design system
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I keep the spacing and colours consistent across the whole page?" The answer is: **manage them centrally with CSS variables — define once, reuse everywhere**. That is the seed of a design system.

items.t: A little JavaScript: dark-mode toggle and nav highlight
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I make the page actually move with JavaScript?" This is the first time we write JS in this book — and if you have learned Python, you will find the syntax very friendly.

items.t: Wrapping up: the checklist and going live
items.s: This lesson answers two questions: "How do I know the page is done?" and "How do I make it reachable by others?" A pre-launch checklist, plus the GitHub Pages deployment flow.

items.t: Variables: `let`, `const` and the `var` Trap
items.s: This lesson settles one question: how do you declare a variable in JS, and why does `var` keep biting people? You already know what a variable is from Python — the JS difference is that there are three ways to declare one, and one of them is a classic footgun.

items.t: `==` vs `===`: the type-coercion trap
items.s: This lesson answers one question: what is the difference between two equals signs and three in JS? `==` performs implicit type conversion and produces some deeply counter-intuitive results. `===` is strict — no conversion, types must match.

items.t: Types and conversion: `NaN`, `typeof null` and string-plus-number
items.s: This lesson answers: how do types actually work in JS? JS is dynamically typed, so a variable can hold a value of any type — but that freedom brings some surprising behaviour. What does `"5" + 3` equal, for example?

items.t: Functions: declarations, expressions and arrow functions
items.s: This lesson answers: what are the several ways to write a function in JS, and how are arrow functions related to Python's `lambda`? You already know Python's `def` and `lambda`; JS's function system is more flexible.

items.t: Arrays and objects: Python's `list` and `dict` compared
items.s: This lesson answers: how do JS arrays and objects work, and how do they differ from Python's lists and dicts? You already know Python's lists and dictionaries; the JS versions are similar, but with some important distinctions.

items.t: Common array methods: `push`/`pop`/`slice`/`splice`
items.s: This lesson answers: what are the common operations on a JS array? You know Python list's `append`, `pop` and slicing; JS has corresponding methods, but with a few key differences.

items.t: Iteration: `for`, `for...of`, `forEach` and the `return` trap
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you iterate over an array in JS? JS offers several styles, and the differences are subtle but important — especially the fact that `return` inside `forEach` does not break out of the loop.

items.t: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`: the functional trio
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you process arrays functionally in JS? You have seen Python's list comprehensions and `map`/`filter`; JS has equivalent methods, and they are pleasantly expressive.

items.t: Objects: create, read, update, delete, iterate, and the missing-property trap
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you create, read, update and delete on a JS object, and how do you iterate over one? You already know that JS objects resemble Python dicts, but they have some distinctive usage patterns worth learning.

items.t: String methods: template literals, `split`/`join`/`includes`
items.s: This lesson answers: what are the common string operations in JS? You know Python's string methods; the JS versions are similar, but with their own flavour — notably template literals.

items.t: What the DOM is: a tree of live objects
items.s: This lesson answers: what exactly is the DOM? This is a concept unique to JS — Python has nothing like it. Understanding the DOM is the foundation of every frontend interaction.

items.t: Finding elements: `getElementById` / `querySelector` / `querySelectorAll`
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you find the element you want inside the DOM tree? This is the first step of every DOM operation — find it first, then manipulate it.

items.t: Changing content: `textContent` vs `innerHTML`
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you change an element's text or HTML content? `textContent` and `innerHTML` can both write content, but their safety and behaviour are completely different.

items.t: Changing attributes and styles: `getAttribute`/`setAttribute`, `classList`, `style`
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you change an element's attributes and CSS styles? You have changed attributes on Python objects before; DOM element attributes and styles work similarly, but with a few dedicated APIs.

items.t: Creating and removing elements: `createElement` / `appendChild` / `remove`
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you create and delete DOM elements dynamically? So far you have only modified elements that already existed. Now you will build elements from scratch and insert them into the page.

items.t: Your first event: `addEventListener`
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you make a page respond to what the user does? A Python script runs top to bottom and then exits. The browser is different: **after your code finishes, the browser keeps waiting** — for clicks, keystrokes, scrolling. That is event-driven programming.

items.t: The event object: `event.target` vs `event.currentTarget`
items.s: This lesson answers: what is that `event` parameter inside your handler, and what is the difference between `target` and `currentTarget`? These two properties are easy to mix up and are the source of many confusing bugs.

items.t: Event delegation: one listener to rule them all
items.s: This lesson answers: when a list has hundreds of items and every item needs a click handler, how do you avoid attaching hundreds of listeners? The answer is event delegation — listen on the parent once and let the event bubble do the routing.

items.t: Common events: `click` / `input` / `submit` / `keydown` and `preventDefault`
items.s: This lesson answers: which events show up most often in real work, how do you use them, and what does `preventDefault` actually do?

items.t: Bubbling and capturing: the three-phase event flow
items.s: This lesson answers: when you click a button, why does its parent also receive the event — and how do you take advantage of that, or stop it?

items.t: Reading form values: inputs, selects, checkboxes and radios
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you get the value the user actually entered or chose? Different controls store their state in different places, and using the wrong property gives you the wrong answer.

items.t: Form validation: required fields, patterns and friendly messages
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you check whether the user's input is valid before sending it, and how do you tell them exactly what to fix?

items.t: `localStorage` and `sessionStorage`: keeping data after a reload
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you store data in the browser so it survives a refresh? The crucial detail is that **storage values are always strings**.

items.t: Console debugging: `log`, `table` and `dir`, breakpoints, and reading the stack
items.s: This lesson answers: when your code does not work, how do you find out why? You will use console output, step through execution with breakpoints, and read a stack trace to locate the real source of an error.

items.t: `setTimeout` and `setInterval`: the asynchronous intuition
items.s: This lesson answers: why does code not run in the order you wrote it? JavaScript schedules callback functions; it does not run them on the spot.

items.t: Project design: breaking down a to-do list into features and data
items.s: This lesson answers: when you are handed a project brief, how do you split it into features, define the data structure, and sketch the interface?

items.t: Structure and style: the HTML skeleton and CSS layout
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you turn last lesson's sketch into actual HTML and CSS?

items.t: CRUD in the browser: render functions and event handling
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you turn the data structure from lesson 26 into a working, interactive to-do app?

items.t: Adding persistence and filters: reading localStorage and rendering by condition
items.s: This lesson answers: how do you make the data survive a refresh, and how do you show only some of it?

items.t: Wrapping up: organising the code and revisiting the classic bugs
items.s: This lesson answers: now that the project works, how do you keep it readable, and why do the same three bugs keep appearing?

items.t: Why We Need Asynchronous Code: JS Single Thread and the Event Loop
items.s: This lesson answers the question "why does `alert` freeze the entire page?" and explains why time-consuming operations must be asynchronous.

items.t: Callbacks: The Original Asynchronous Pattern and Callback Hell
items.s: This lesson covers callbacks — the original form of asynchrony in JavaScript — and why too much nesting becomes "hell."

items.t: Promises: Three States and Chaining
items.s: This lesson covers what a Promise is, its three states, and how `.then`/`.catch` flatten callback hell into a chain.

items.t: async/await: Writing Asynchronous Code Synchronously
items.s: This lesson covers the `async/await` syntax sugar and the critical performance concept of "parallel execution."

items.t: Error Handling: try/catch with await and finally
items.s: This lesson covers how to catch errors in asynchronous code, and how to avoid letting `.catch` "swallow" errors.

items.t: fetch Basics: GET Requests and the Response Object
items.s: This lesson covers the basic usage of the browser-native `fetch` API, with a focus on how to extract values from the `Response` object.

items.t: POST Requests and Headers: method, headers, body
items.s: This lesson covers how to send POST requests with `fetch`, and why `JSON.stringify` is required.

items.t: fetch Does Not Reject on HTTP 404/500
items.s: This is the classic `fetch` pitfall: **network-level success ≠ business-level success**. You must manually check `res.ok`.

items.t: Loading States and Error Handling: Three States and AbortController
items.s: This lesson covers the essential "three-state management" of any real application, and how to cancel a request that has already been sent.

items.t: Real-World Practice: A Small App Using a Real API and CORS
items.s: This lesson ties together the first four lessons by building a small app that calls a public API, and explains what cross-origin requests are all about.

items.t: JSON Deep Cloning, Circular References, and structuredClone
items.s: This lesson covers the "deep clone" problem for objects, and the classic `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` trick — along with its fatal flaws.

items.t: Map and Set: Knowing When to Use Them Instead of Object / Array
items.s: This lesson covers two "enhanced" data structures: Map (key-value pairs) and Set (unique-value collections), and when you should reach for them instead of Object/Array.

items.t: localStorage Advanced: Capacity, Version Migration, and JSON.parse Safety
items.s: This lesson covers advanced localStorage usage, with a focus on how to avoid "reading corrupt data and crashing the entire page."

items.t: IndexedDB: When to Use It and When Not To
items.s: This lesson gives you a "storage selection map" so you can understand the boundary between IndexedDB and localStorage.

items.t: Data Sync: Local Cache + Network Updates, and Optimistic Updates
items.s: This lesson covers common patterns in real applications: displaying the cache first then updating from the network, and "pretending it succeeded" with optimistic updates.

items.t: Destructuring, Spread, Optional Chaining and Nullish Coalescing
items.s: This lesson covers four bits of syntax that make code shorter and safer at the same time: destructuring, spread, `?.` and `??`.

items.t: Iterators and Generators: Building the Intuition First
items.s: This lesson skips the spec details and focuses on one idea: **a generator is a function you can pause**, yielding values one at a time.

items.t: Classes and Modules: `class` and ES Modules
items.s: This lesson covers two tools for organising code: the object-oriented style of `class`, and splitting files apart with `import`/`export`.

items.t: New Array Tricks: flat / flatMap / Object.fromEntries / at
items.s: This lesson covers a handful of array and object methods that make code shorter and nicer to read.

items.t: Debounce and Throttle: The Most Practical Lesson in This Book
items.s: This lesson covers two tools for controlling how often a function runs: debounce and throttle, including the async cases.

items.t: Canvas Basics: getContext, Coordinates and Rectangles
items.s: This lesson builds the basic intuition for Canvas: it's a bitmap drawing surface, and everything you draw goes through a "drawing context" object.

items.t: Canvas Paths and Shapes: beginPath / moveTo / lineTo / arc / fill / stroke
items.s: This lesson covers Canvas's "path" mechanism — the foundation for drawing any shape (lines, circles, polygons).

items.t: Canvas Text and Images: fillText, Fonts, Chinese Fonts, and measureText
items.s: This lesson covers writing text and drawing images on a canvas, plus the unavoidable problems of "Chinese won't display" and "text layout".

items.t: Canvas Animation: requestAnimationFrame and the Animation Loop
items.s: This lesson covers how to make a Canvas move, and why `requestAnimationFrame` beats `setInterval` for animation.

items.t: Hands-on: Drawing a Simple Bar Chart with Canvas
items.s: This lesson ties everything together: axes, ticks, bars, and labels, all drawn by hand with Canvas.

items.t: Project Design: Breaking Down a Weather and Exchange-Rate App
items.s: This lesson writes no code. It figures out what we're building first — requirements, data structures, API choices, and a wireframe sketch, in four steps.

items.t: Structure and Styling: the HTML Skeleton and CSS Layout
items.s: This lesson turns last chapter's sketch into real HTML and CSS, with an emphasis on semantic structure and state switching.

items.t: Connecting to Real APIs: fetch + async/await + Error Handling + Loading State
items.s: This lesson wires the frontend to a real endpoint: fetching data with fetch, writing it with async/await, and handling errors and loading states properly.

items.t: Adding Cache, Debounced Search, and Request Race Handling
items.s: This lesson solves three common real-world problems: storing results in localStorage, not searching on every keystroke, and handling "late responses arriving early."

items.t: Wrapping Up: Code Organisation, Performance, Accessibility, and What's Next
items.s: The final lesson turns the project from "it runs" into "it's maintainable": splitting modules, tightening performance, caring about accessibility, and learning to debug.

items.t: What Code Actually Is
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How does the text I type turn into a running program?" Once you understand how the browser runs your code, you will know where to look when something goes wrong.

items.t: Variables: Labels You Stick on Boxes
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How does a program remember anything?" A variable is the name you give to a piece of data. Remember the name and you can pull the data back out whenever you need it.

items.t: Data Types: What Is Actually Inside the Box
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "What can I put in a variable?" Numbers, text, and true/false values are all different kinds of data, and the kind decides what you can do with it.

items.t: Numbers vs Strings: Why "3" + "4" = "34"
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "Why on earth does `'3' + '4'` give me `'34'`?" This is the most famous trap in JavaScript, and understanding it will save you from an entire class of bugs.

items.t: Output and Debugging: Making Your Program Tell You What It Did
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I know what my code is doing wrong?" Learning to read error messages and print things out means you can solve most problems by yourself.

items.t: Comparisons: Teaching Your Program to Make Judgements
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How does a program decide whether something is true?" Comparison operators are the foundation of the `if` statement, and the difference between `=` and `===` is the single biggest trap for a beginner.

items.t: If / Else: Making Your Program Choose
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I make a program do different things in different situations?" `if / else` is the most basic branch in programming, exactly like the everyday "if this, then that; otherwise, do something else."

items.t: AND, OR and NOT: Combining Conditions
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I combine several checks?" It is like saying "cheap **and** good quality" -- both have to hold. Or "VIP **or** on sale" -- either one is enough.

items.t: The for Loop: Repeating Work Without Writing It Twice
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I make the computer do the same thing over and over?" The `for` loop is one of the most-used tools in programming — counting to 10, going through a list, repeating an action, they all rely on it.

items.t: The while Loop and Picking the Right Kind
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "When should I use while instead of for?" Both loops repeat work, but each one fits a different situation. Understanding the difference helps you write code that feels natural.

items.t: Arrays: A Row of Numbered Boxes
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I store a whole bunch of things at once?" A variable holds one value, but an array holds a whole list of values, kept in order.

items.t: Changing an Array: Adding, Removing, and Editing
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I add things to an array, take things out, or change what is inside?" `push`, `pop`, and `splice` are the workhorses of array manipulation, and together with a loop they handle almost any list-based task.

items.t: Objects: One Thing with Several Labels
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I describe one specific thing?" An array is great for a list of similar items, but an object bundles together several facts about one thing — name, age, city — in one place.

items.t: Arrays of Objects: What Real Data Looks Like
items.s: This lesson answers the question: "How do I store a whole list of structured records?" In real projects, the data you get back from a server is almost always an "array of objects" — an array where each item is itself an object.

items.t: Putting It All Together: A Class Roster
items.s: This lesson ties together everything you have learned so far. You are going to build a small project: managing a class roster with arrays and objects — adding, listing, filtering, and counting.

items.t: What a Function Is: Wrapping Up a Block of Code
items.s: For the first 15 lessons, your code ran top to bottom, one line after another. From this lesson on we learn **functions**: they wrap a block of code and give it a name, so you can run it whenever you call that name. It is one of the most valuable habits in programming.

items.t: Parameters: Making Functions Reusable
items.s: So far every function we wrote did exactly the same thing each time. This lesson introduces **parameters** — the feature that lets a function "swallow different data and produce different results." This is where functions become genuinely useful.

items.t: Return Values: The Function's Output Chute
items.s: Every function we have written so far just `console.log`-ed its result. In real projects you usually want to "calculate something and hand it back" so the caller can use it. This lesson covers `return`.

items.t: Scope: Where a Variable Lives
items.s: Why can't you use a variable declared inside a function from the outside? And why *can* a function read a variable declared outside it? This lesson explains **scope** so you never get blindsided by a `ReferenceError` again.

items.t: Array Methods: forEach / map / filter
items.s: In lesson 13 we used a `for` loop to walk through an array. This lesson introduces three built-in array methods that do the same job with less code and better readability. We focus on building intuition first; the callback details will come later.

items.t: The Web Page Is a Tree: What the DOM Is
items.s: Every line of JavaScript we have written so far ran in the "console." From this chapter on, JS gets to work with real elements on a web page — clicking buttons, changing text, adding list items. All of that relies on the **DOM**.

items.t: Finding Elements: `querySelector` / `querySelectorAll`
items.s: Last lesson we learned that `document` is the entry point. This lesson is about "how to find an element inside the DOM tree" — the prerequisite for every operation that follows.

items.t: Reading and Changing Content: `textContent` vs `innerHTML`
items.s: Once you have found an element, the most common thing to do is "read its text" or "change its text." This lesson covers the two properties people mix up most often — and one serious security risk.

items.t: Changing Styles: `classList` and Editing `style` Directly
items.s: This lesson covers two ways to change styling. The preferred one is `classList` — toggling a class on and off — with direct `style` edits kept for quick, one-off fixes. Learn the first well and your styles stay manageable.

items.t: Events: `addEventListener` and Why Not `onclick`
items.s: A web page is not a program that "runs once and ends." It is a program that "waits for the user to click." This lesson is about events: how to make JavaScript react when the user clicks, types, or moves the mouse.

items.t: Chapter 6 Capstone Project (26–30)
items.s: Starting from this lesson, we build a real web project: a To-Do List. It is the classic beginner exercise in frontend, and it ties together everything from the first 25 lessons. The first step is not writing code — it is getting the requirements straight.

items.t: Structure and Styles: Build the Shell First
items.s: Last lesson fixed the data and the functions. This lesson puts up the page "skeleton" and its "look" — the input box, the button, and the list container. The logic stays empty for now; we get the structure working first.

items.t: Rendering the List: Turning an Array into Elements on the Page
items.s: Last lesson put up the shell. This lesson implements `render()`: it turns every item in the `todos` array into an `<li>` on the page. This is the core step of the whole project.

items.t: Adding and Deleting: Add One, Remove One, and Re-render After Every Change
items.s: Last lesson implemented render. This lesson finishes the two features "add" and "delete" — and now the whole to-do list runs. The core is just one sentence: **after changing the array, re-render.**

items.t: The Final Lesson: Code Organisation, Common Bugs, and What Comes Next
items.s: This is the last lesson of *Web Design · JavaScript from Scratch (Slow Track)*. It organises the whole project's code, reviews three common bugs, and tells you what to learn next.

items.t: Why Automate: How Long to Rename 200 Files Manually
items.s: This lesson helps you do the math: how much time repetitive work really wastes, and how a script makes it trivial.

items.t: Walking Directories: `os.walk` / `pathlib.iterdir`, Filtering by Extension
items.s: This lesson covers step 1 of batch processing: how to "find" files in a directory and pick only the ones we want.

items.t: Batch Renaming: String Handling, `Path.rename`, Preview First
items.s: This lesson covers steps 2 and 3: computing the new name, then actually renaming — but **print the plan and confirm before touching anything**.

items.t: Sorting by Rules: By Extension/Date, `shutil.move`
items.s: This lesson is about taking scattered files and sorting them into folders by rule — the start of a real Downloads-folder organizer.

items.t: Project: Organize the Downloads Folder (Preview, Then Act)
items.s: This lesson ties the first four together into a genuinely usable "Downloads organizer", applying "preview before execute" throughout.

items.t: Reading Spreadsheets: `openpyxl` Basics, Cells, Rows & Columns
items.s: This lesson enters the world of spreadsheets: opening a workbook with `openpyxl` and understanding the three basic concepts — cell, row, column.

items.t: Iterating and Summarizing: Sum, Count, Max
items.s: This lesson reads a spreadsheet and runs statistics — summing, counting, finding the max. This is the foundation of automated reporting.

items.t: Writing Spreadsheets: New Workbook, Writing, Saving
items.s: Done reading — now writing: create a spreadsheet, fill it in, save as .xlsx.

items.t: Merging Sheets: Combining Many Files into One
items.s: This lesson solves a common need: one sheet per month, then at year end combine all 12 into one — entirely scripted.

items.t: Project: Build a Monthly Report (Read Many → Summarize → Output)
items.s: This lesson ties lessons 6–9 together: read multiple detail sheets, summarize by item, output a clean monthly report.
